speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg leave, subject to the approval of the House, to introduce a Bill, and I ask the House to waive the requirement of previous notice. The purpose of the Bill is to ratify and confirm certain proceedings in connection with plebiscites that have taken place under part 4 of the Canada Temperance Act. As the House is doubtless aware, there is pending presently before the Supreme Court an action in which the proceedings in the province of Alberta are attacked. Numerous constitutional grounds are invoked, and of course with those this Bill is not concerned. But I understand, that it is further claimed that there was an irregularity in the original proclamation ordering the plebiscite, the alleged irregularity consisting in the fact that that proclamation did not state a specific day on which the prohibition would come into effect if the vote of the people was favourable to it. The proclamation stated that the prohibition would come into effect, in the event of the vote being favourable, on a day to be fixed by a subsequent Order in Council. Our law officers were then, and still are, of opinion that the proclamation in its present form is sufficient; but in view of the obvious, I think I may say, prejudice to the general public interests if the case should be de-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
termined upon this mere question of regularity, and determined in a sense adverse to the validity of the election, it seems to us wise that that minor question should be removed subject to such conditions, of course, as will do no injustice to the parties ' in the case whatever be the event of the judgment. The Bill contains two clauses. The first clause deals with this particular question of the proclamation, and the second clause is one of general application analogous to a clause already existing in the general Elections Act, substantially providing that no mere defect of form shall invalidate any order given under the Canada Temperance Act pursuant to a plebiscite, unless it appears that the result of the vote has been, by reason of the irregularity complained of, materially altered. This last clause, as I say, is analogous although not in identical words, to a similar clause, proceeding upon the same principle contained in the general Elections Act, and I think it is a clause which will commend itself to the judgment of the members of this House. Taking this particular instance, should it happen that the result of the present proceedings should be a judgment setting aside all that has been done upon the ground of what is claimed to be an irregularity, the country would find itself in this position, that it would be necessary to begin all over again; incur the entire expense of the plebiscite, and furthermore with the prospect-more than the prospect, I think one might say the certainty-that we would have, in connection with the constitutional question involved, the now pending action, which has now reached the Supreme Court, to be gone all over again. All this would entail considerable expense to the parties, and more especially to the country, and would attain no substantial advantage or benefit for any one. It is not, from what we can ascertain, probable that a judgment will be rendered before Parliament prorogues, and if a judgment comes after prorogation, and resting upon this alleged irregularity, there would be no opportunity to take any action for a long period of months, and there would certainly be no opportunity then, by any action that would be taken, to obtain a judgment upon the constitutional questions in the present case. We would then find ourselves with an interregnum of indecision. We might possibly ratify the plebiscite at that time, but it would still be subject to attack upon the . constitutional grounds that are invoked. From every point of view it seems to be 
desirable that the matter should be dealt with upon these important constitutional points, and that we should run no risk of its going off upon a mere question of formality, and of a judgment being rendered which, if it rests solely upon that question of formality, will leave all the parties interested, and the country, in the position I have indicated, and subject both to very heavy costs.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unless the right hon gentleman gets the unanimous consent ol the House he cannot proceed. Is it the pleasure of the House that the right hon. gentleman should have unanimous consent to introduce this Bill?

I ask the privilege of
putting a question. Is it the intention of the right hon. gentleman to legislate people out of court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We propose not to legislate them out of court, but the effect of our legislation would be to determine that particular question.

Instead of the court
determining it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The court would decide what is regular under the existing law, the effect of the Bill would be to modify the law so as to obviate the necessity of deciding that question. So far as the particular parties in the case are concerned, their one interest in its being done now or later is in regard to the costs they have incurred, and the Bill specially provides that the court shall determine, whatever may be its ultimate decision, as to the question of costs.

Does that apply to
pending cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It does not say so in
express words.
It is not unanimous.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) objects. Therefore the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Doherty) not getting unanimous consent, his further proceeding would be out of order.

Give notice. I do not
object now, but I will later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I had reason to believe that it would not be objected to.

speechtext: Hon. S. F. TOLMIE (Minister of Agriculture) moved the third reading of Bill No. 205, to amend the Oleomargarine Act,, 1919.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon, W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :	Mr. Speaker, I have no desire
to delay the House for many minutes, but I really think this Bill should not pass its final stage without a brief comment upon the extraordinary position which the Government have taken in relation to it. The question whether oleomargarine is a legitimate article of trade and commerce was long ago answered by all the world, with one exception, and that exception was the Dominion of Canada. While the rest of the world has decided that oleomargarine, whatever its merit may be as a foodstuff, is a legitimate article of trade and commerce, Canada has declined hitherto to reach that conclusion. The Government, however, have not declined; the Government have come to the conclusion that Canada should not isolate herself from the rest of the world, from the rest of civilization. The Government, from their own testimony, have come to the conclusion that oleomargarine is a legitimate article of trade and commerce. It is not a new question; the Government have had it before them for some years, and after years of discussion they decided that the ban should be removed and the article allowed to be traded in the same as any other. But, while the Government tell us that is their conclusion, unhappily they have not the courage to stand by it. Unfortunately, while the House was ready to support them, while many on this side were ready to support them, the Government suddenly lost all faith in their own Bill. Now, for those hon. members representing farming communities who thought that in the interests of their farmers they should oppose this Bill, one can have profound respect. As for those members who opposed the Bill very warmly and then voted for it, I do not care to make any comment. But the attitude of the Government in the matter is a most extraordinary one. They tell us they have reached the conclusion that there is no further ground for putting a ban on oleomargarine, yet they are going to pass a Bill which will permit the importation, manufacture and sale of this product for one year only and bring about another fight in another year. The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) said last night that he was satisfied with the Bill as originally introduced. Well, if the Government held that view why did they change it? As to hon. gentlemen on that side who opposed the Bill, the Government should have known better than to take them seriously. The Government should have known very well that when it IMr. Tolmie.]
came to a division those hon. members would stand loyally by them. But at the first sign of opposition the Government suddenly threw up their hands-it is the old story of Davy Crockett and the coon: "Don't shoot; I'll come down". When the House was ready to support the Bill, when everything pointed to a settlement of this long-standing question, hon. gentlemen pursued this extraordinary course. It was an exhibition of indecision, of weakness and of folly which will not inure to the credit of the Canadian Government.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: House again in committee on Bill No. 138, to amend the Criminal Code-Right Hon. Mr. Doherty-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House was last in committee upon this Bill clause 1 had been allowed to stand and clause 2 had been dropped, clauses 3 and 4 had been adopted and we wTere considering clause 5.

I understand that clause
5 incorporates in the Bill the legislation which was introduced by the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The wording is not
identical, but I think the same purpose is sought to be attained. I understand, however, that the hon. member for North Simcoe desired to move an amendment. I do not understand it to be of material consequence, but as he is not in his seat at the moment, and as I should like to afford him an opportunity at all events of putting his proposed amendment before the committee, perhaps we might let this clause stand and go on with the others in the meantime.

I do not think that clause 5 as it stands is nearly as definite as was the Bill introduced by the hon. member for North Simcoe. Last year this House passed an amendment to the Criminal Code which was not very well understood by members of the House who were then present. It was understood that the amendment would make it illegal for a foreigner or alien to have firearms in his possession. Unfortunately this amendment did not so apply; it makes it illegal for any person, any Canadian, to have in his possession a gun, rifle, cannon or anything of that kind, without a permit.

In the majority of cases this permit is to be issued by officers who are stipendiary magistrates, police magistrates, or chiefs of police. As the law stands at present the permits are valid only within the jurisdiction of the officer who issues them. That means that if a man starts out on a hunting trip, say, from Ottawa and has to go through various counties in the province of Quebec, he may be arrested for having arms illegally in his possession the moment he leaves Ottawa, and at any time thereafter unless he gets a permit from each district through which he passes having jurisdiction in such matters. I do not think that was the intention of Parliament at all, and I would say that we should simply repeal clause (aa), the provision I complain of, and put nothing in its place.

I would
like to endorse what the member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) has said. The amendment of last year has created a great deal of annoyance and hardship and I would like to see the provision removed before the end of this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There will be discussion upon this section, so I suggest again that the clause stand and we may go on with those sections which do not give rise to discussion.
Section stands.
On section 6-illicit connection with Indian women:
In what respect is a change being made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is to make it an offence for any white man to have illicit connection with an Indian woman.
Was that not tie law before?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Illicit connection between a man and a woman is not a crime save in certain particular cases-as regards girls of certain ages and so forth. This is to make fornication of a white man with an Indian woman an offence. It is proposed in response to the strong urge af Indian agents and persons responsible for conditions upon reserves. It is represented that the consequences of illicit connection between the squaw and the white man which, I regret to say, is reported as being exceedingly prevalent, are most disastrous upon the reserves and to the tribes. As I have said it is represented to us that
there ought to be special legislation that would enable efforts to be made to mitigate or, it is hoped, entirely to suppress this regrettable practice.
Does this apply to cases of Indians living on reserves, or otherwise? Or to both?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the clause stands, it applies to any Indian woman. It is not specially limited to a woman on a reserve, and if it is a good disposition, even though the abuse be more evident upon the reserve, I think there is no need to limit the disposition to the particular places where we see the evidence of the evil consequences.
It applies without "reserve."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Would it apply to halL breeds?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not before me the Indian Act which, I understand, contains a clause defining the status of a halfbreed. It would depend upon the definition whether a half-breed is to be treated as an Indian or not. In certain cases he is treated as an Indian. It would apply to whoever, under the law, is an Indian and to nobody else.

Last year we passed an Act for the compulsory enfranchisement of Indians. When the Indian acquires a certain standard of living or civilization, the law provides now that he may be enfranchised against his will. When this process is adopted with regard to Indians, will this clause apply to Indian women after they have been enfranchised under the law passed last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, and I am quite prepared to amend the provision by making it read: "with any unenfranchised Indian female."
Why should the change be made? Does enfranchisement increase their mentality, or make them more virtuous, or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, but it puts them on the footing of the every-day, ordinary citizen. We must treat them as Indians or as non-Indians, and if by enfranchisement we make them non-Indians for all other purposes, I hardly think we should continue to treat them as Indians for this one particular purpose.



*__________________________
The question would then become one of-When is an Indian not an Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
When he is enfranchised.

This clause is objectionable in another way. I think it provides an inducement for blackmail. As the clause stands, there is nothing to prevent any Indian female laying a charge against a white man and having her buck Indian coming behind her for the few dollars and holding up the white man. I think the clause will- do more harm than good. We do not want to give the buck Indian an opportunity, by such legislation, to take money out of white people's pockets.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose that is a possible evil. It is a thing that may occur with regard to crime of any nature. You may have combinations to charge people falsely with offences. If you are dealing with the case1 of an innocent man, I should think it would be difficult to establish a case. If you are dealing with the case of a guilty man, even though the purpose of those who are prosecuting is to get money, the fact remains that he is guilty of an offence of a nature which, it would appear if representations made are correct, there is a special necessity for endeavouring to suppress.
What are the representations for this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The representations
are that there is a practical disregard on the part of white men of any obligation to respect these Indian women, and on the other hand the Indian women are, perhaps, not as alive as women of other races in the country to the importance of maintaining their chastity, and so forth. What is pointed out, I understand, is not so much the consequences to the individual Indian woman, as the consequences to the tribe as a whole of the prevalence of this apparently recognized practice or malpractice. .

I do not think the evil that this legislation is intended to check is going to be equal to the dangers to which this clause is open. As a rule. Indian women, particularly out in the West, have their bucks to look after them, and they are pretty jealous of and able to look after their women. We are going to legislate for human beings; we are going to 
pass a law that is going to expose the white man to be the victim of an Indian woman. The better method would be to have legislation on the reserve and to see that the Indians are properly looked after by the people in charge of the reserve Let them educate the bucks to look after their own women. That would be more humanitarian than to entice them to learn new tricks to hold up the white man and blackmail him.

Blackmail is a white
man's offence. I do not think it can be found to any extent amongst others than white people, so that there is not much danger of that.
We do not want any legislation that will engender that evil amongst the Indians.
Having regard to what has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) as regards the Indians, I am bound to say that I deprecate this proposed legislation. More harm than good will result from it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in any sense absolutely tied up to this legislation. I was endeavouring to meet the views of those who seemed to be in the best position to judge.
Who are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The officers of the Indian Department in charge of the reserves. It seems to me that the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is arguing against this Bill from totally different premises. In the first place he suggests the buck Indian coming behind his squaw, joining with her to prosecute the white man in order to get some money out of him. In the next place he says that the buck Indian is so jealous of his wife that there is no need to afford her any other protection. The hon. member must have two buck Indians in mind, a different buck Indian for each speech. However, if the sense of this committee is that there should be a further examination of this provision, I shall not insist on pressing it through at the present time. On the other hand, for myself I feel disposed, from representations made to me, to think that this is good legislation, and I would not like to drop it unless I felt that the sense of the committee generally was against it
Section dropped.

On section 7-falsely registering at hotels, etc., as man and -wife:
Is not this the clause that was dropped by the Senate last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

It was dropped by the
Senate for three successive years. The department seems to overlook the fact that the Senate is not in agreement with the Commons on this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Our experience has
been that the Senate has not been in agreement with the Commons on certain questions, but that they have had respect for the perseverance of the Commons, and have come to agree on being given repeated opportunities of seeing the error of their ways. I think that this House, having already more than once committed itself to the desirability of this provision, would be only acting consistently in passing it again. We have had experience of rejection by the Senate of certain provisions at one or more sessions and of the Senate finally, perhaps because of our importunity, yielding and passing the legislation.
By the process of attrition, I suppose-wearing them out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Contrition.

I opposed this measure when it came up three years ago; I opposed it when it came up two years ago; I opposed it last year, and I have not seen anything to change my views since. The question of blackmail would often arise in such a case, if it does not in the case of the Indian woman. The clause before the committee reads:
Every one is guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars or six months' imprisonment, who at any hotel, boarding or lodging house, whether by registering in any book kept in such hotel, boarding or lodging house, or otherwise, represents or pretends that a woman or man is his wife or husband, as the case may be, knowing the same to be untrue, and the onus of proof of the absence of knowledge shall be upon the person accused. I
I would direct the attention of the committee to this curious clause. It is no offence for a man and a woman to cohabit. They can live together for thirty years in open adultery to the scandal of the whole community, and that is not an offence under our law, nor is it made an offence under this clause; 'but as soon as they register
at an hotel they are liable to a fine of $500 or six months' imprisonment. Is not that absurd? Make the act of cohabitation an offence and I might be willing to support it, but to make that act of registration an offence seems to me to be absurd on the face of it. The people may be perfectly respectable citizens and commit no offence so long as they cohabit in their house, but as soon as they register at an hotel, a crime is committed. I should like to know what is the crime of registration? If the law will condone living together in open concubinage and adultery, why will it not overlook the offence of registration? Suppose this lady and gentleman want to paper their house and have to move out in the meantime to a boarding house or a hotel. Under this clause they are liable to six months' imprisonment for moving out of their house. The legislation is absurd, and the whole tenor of it is in the direction of bringing our law into ridicule and contempt. I understand that it is being promoted and fostered by some hysterical woman's society, who think they can make people virtuous by act of Parliament. I am opposed to this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman suggests that we should pass a law making cohabitation or adultery an offence, that is one question. My hon. friend did not quite commit himself as to whether he would support such legislation. The evil that is sought to be struck at here is the utilization of places of public resort, like hotels, boarding or lodging houses, for the purpose of committing the sin of adultery. It is represented that this is applicable on the large lines to a class of cases quite different from that which the hon. member suggests ; that is to say, it affords opportunity for what I might call casual cohabitation-
Accidental.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Accidental cohabitation of people who have no permanent liaison of any kind between them. It is a public scandal when it becomes a matter of general knowledge that a certain hotel in a community is a place where any couple can go and register as man and wife, and have all the liberties thereto pertaining. It does seem to me that that is an evil distinct from-I do not say a greater evil than-the sin of adultery itself. This provision has been urged, I might say, by people who are neither women, nor, so far as it is possible for me to judge, hysterical, and whose work is practically constantly

connected with the endeavour to suppress offences against morality. They look upon the immunity which at present exists in this case as being very detrimental to the general morals of the community in which this practice prevails.

Is not this legislation
just about on the same line as the Mann Act which was passed in the United States some years ago? Perhaps the right hon. gentleman knows that that Act has been a most fruitful source of blackmail, to such an extent that it has been condemned even in the States where it was originally in force. In the face of that experience, I do not see why we in this House should endeavour to pass legislation which has failed hopelessly in the United States. There is no question that this legislation will lead to the results far worse than the supposed crime that it is intended to stop. The right hon. gentleman has said that this House has assented to this clause once or twice before. The last time this Bill went through the House was at the end of the session, when nobody paid any particular attention to it. So far as I am concerned, I distinctly object to this class of legislation. I think it leads to offences which are far worse than the evil intended to be cured, and for that reason I stoutly oppose this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is another clause in respect of which I am quite in the hands of the committee. I have heard no expression of opinion favourable to the clause, and I desire to call attention to that on the part of hon. gentlemen who have sat silent. If there be any view favourable to the clause, I think it ought to express itself. I do not want personally, alone, to stand for insisting on a provision of this kind, if the committee generally are against it.

There are very many reasons, I think, why this clause should be passed, particularly in view of the many travellers who come to our summer resorts in Ontario, and I suppose in the other provinces, in the summer. Couples travelling in this way from the United States and from the cities of Canada will put up at hotels, and they become practically a nuisance to the people who are spending the summer in the community with their children. It is not the class of people that should go to these summer resorts or, for that matter, to any of the hotels, and it seems to me that unless something is done

to prevent a recurrence of this, matters will become worse. The summer season is prolific in that sort of thing, and, while I do not suppose that summer resorts are subjected to this trouble to any greater extent than any other class of hotel, yet I think that this practice is increasing, and something along the line proposed should be adopted in order to stop it.

I support the minister in this matter, and I shall vote for the law he proposes because I think it is necessary. I have considerable experience of what passes in Montreal, having been Crown Prosecutor for sixteen years now. I have consulted the magistrates and they are all of the opinion that this law is absolutely necessary. As the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) says, it is too bad to see people living in immorality, and I will add that we should do everything we can to curtail the practice. We should try, if ve can, to keep the hotels and boarding houses, as far as possible, free of this sort of thing. In the light of my experience gained in Montreal, I can do nothing bui vote for this law

In a great
many of these matters, it is very essential that governments and legislative bodies should draw a clear distinction between crime and sin. I come from-a country where law is administered, as I think it is throughout the British Empire, with the utmost care and rigour; but law is for the repression of < rime, especially crime committed against other people. It is not the function of government to cure sin; preachers and gospels have been labouring with sinners ever since the fall of man, and that is their function. I repeat, it is not the funct;cn of governments to cure sin. There are only three possible things we can do with the sinner, whatever the sin. You could hang him or her, but that would be a very drastic cure for most sins, and I am afraid we should find it difficult to procure executioners. And you could confine all sinners; but there, again, you would be met with the difficulty of finding gaol space and gaolers. If you do not hang them, and you do not confine them, then it follows that the sinners must live somewhere; and where governments have made tremendous blunders, blunders leading to enormous evil difficult to calculate, is that they have tried too much to make regulations as to where these peopL should live. I think the point raised by my hon. friend from George Etienne Car-

' tier was well taken, namely, that the real crime that is being raised in this Act is the "crime" of registration. In effect it is said: Adultery is all right, but you mus: not associate it with spring cleaning,- and that is the whole thing with the minister. The minister admits that he cannot do anything wi'h adultery; but if adultery be associated with spring cleaning, necessitating the removal of people for the time being to somewhere else than where they were before, then they immediately become proteges and clinical clients of my right hon. friend. I hope the minister will not extend his operations too far in this handling of sinners from the legal point of view. If he did. he could begin in comparatively near proximity to himself, and find some eligible subjects for his paternal solicitude. I horn stly think that this paternalistic legislation has gone a little bit too far, and this law might very well wait fo-a while.
Section negatived on division
On section 8-driving a motor vehie'e while intoxicated made an offence.
What is the meaning of the term "intoxicated" in this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the courts have frequent occasion to determine when a man is intoxicated or drunk, and I do not fancy there is any more difficulty in deciding when the driver of an automobile is intoxicated than there is in establishing the drunkenness of any person not so engaged. If my hon. friend thinks the word "drunk' would be more clear, I shall insert it. I have a recollection of a policeman who was charged with being drunk on duty, and who pleaded that he might have been personally intoxicated, but that he was not officially drank. I do not know whether my hon. friend would make any such distinction.

There are different de grees of drunkenness. There are cases where a man may be slightly intoxicated, but not to a sufficient extent to interfere with his driving a motor vehicle, while in other cases, he might be so affected as not to be able to handle the wheel at all. We should mention the degree of intoxication from which he is suffering before making It an offence.
Twenty glasses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Does not the hon. member think that if a man came before the court and the evidence was that, although
he had something to drink, he was not so intoxicated as to affect his control over a motor vehicle, the court would hold, under those circumstances, that he was not intoxicated or drunk?

My experience with
*[DOT]courts leads me to think that we should not leave too much to the discretion of the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not leave too
much, but I think we ought to leave a little.
Yes, a little.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are leaving very
little in this instance. There are similar provisions imposing penalties, I think in some of the provinces.
In Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would point out the
great gravity there is in a man driving a motor vehicle while in such a state as not to be able to control himself, to say nothing of the vehicle, and thus exposing the lives of the population. The dangers to which we are all exposed do not come so much from our own carelessness as from the carelessness of others, and this is true in the case of accidents in connection with motor vehicles. In- connection with the Ticket of Leave Act, and other legislation of that kind, I have been startled at the frequency of offences in which people are killed or seriously maimed because of carelessness in the driving of motor cars, and under those circumstances it is, in my judgment, a very serious offence for a man, in any degree of intoxication that affects his perfect carefulness, undertaking to run a motor car. I do not think that the proposed penalty is too great.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9,-Age that consent of child no defence in indecent assault raised from 14 to 16.

What is the purpose of
raising the age limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is simply to assimilate the case of indecent assault with the case of illicit connection. The law previously fixed at 14 the age limit at which it was an offence to have connection with a girl. It has been raised with the' consent of the Senate to 16. Now with regard to cases of indecent assault, where the consent is no defence, when the law stood that the completion of the act of illicit connection, regardless of consent, was a crime only with regard to girls under fourteen, then it was logical and consistent that the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
age limit with regard to cases of indecent assault in which consent would not be a defence should be fourteen. But having raised the age with regard to the grave offence referred to it would only be consistent to make the same alteration with regard to indecent assault.	„
Section agreed to.
On section 10-Whipping added to punishments for rape.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the law stands at
the present time we have the anomalous situation that you may whip a man for attempting to commit rape, but you may not whip him if he succeeds.
Except that he is imprisoned for life.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He may be imprisoned
for life, but he may not be whipped, whereas for the mere attempt he may be whipped.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	There is one thing I
would like to say about the punishment of whipping before this section is passed. The courts, both here and in the Old Country, hear appeals in the most serious criminal offences. A man is found guilty by judge and jury of murder, nevertheless he has the right of appeal and he has a chance of escaping; but whenever a whipping is applied there is no good talking about an appeal, and there may not be a chance of getting a stay of proceedings. I am opposed to whipping at all on that ground. I am strongly with the Minister of Justice as to any reasonable punishment, but I take that objection to whipping. If the whipping is once applied there is no remedy for it, there is nothing you can do about it. I am told by those who have seen flogging or whipping that it is a most beastly thing, and on principle I must register my protest against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There will always be
applications to remit that penalty. We have numerous applications to remit the whipping even when there is no request to remit the imprisonment. These applications are always very carefully considered and there is, of course, that remedy.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-Provision respecting carnally knowing girl between 14 and 16.

How will the section
read now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In 1920 this House
raised the age.
You have at present the provision that the girl must previously be of chaste character and now you are striking that out?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Will you explain the
reason for striking it out?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
For the same reasons
that we did not put it in when we passed the law. The section as it was passed by this House was that:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for live years who carnally knows any girl under the age of 16 and above the age of 14 not being his wife, and whether he believes her to be above the age of 16 or not.
The Senate modified that provision by inserting a requirement that the girl should have been of previous chaste character. Now that is a requirement that has existed in connection with other offences of! a similar nature and which has given rise to a very great deal of difficulty in the application of the law. It has involved, necessarily involved, in every case of this kind an investigation into the chastity of the girl who has been the victim. Whatever you may say, when you are dealing with girls under sixteen, the man who takes the responsibility of having illicit connection with a girl under that age, might, I think, very well be subjected to some measure of punishment without an investigation of the entire past life of the girl concerned.

What if the man is
fifteen or sixteen years of age or less?
Yes, young boys.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well if he is fifteen
or sixteen years of age he has not done a very virtuous thing has he?
I am ready to admit that, nor has she.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And the court will
consider all these circumstances in the measuring out of the punishment. We have got to make a general law, and the one question that we are concerned with now is, whether the existence of the offence should turn upon the previous chastity of the girl. As I have said, in the application of the law a situation is created where a girl, who has been wronged in this way, must submit, if she consents to a prosecution, to being brought before the court and humiliated by all sorts of endeavours to find out whether or not she has, at any previous occasion or time,

misbehaved herself, all for the purpose of trying to procure the escape from punishment of a person -who admittedly has been guilty of a sin. I would not like to arouse the indignation of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), but after all if the law should not suppress sin-and I quite agree we might have, as in our charitable operations perhaps, to begin at home if we are going to absolutely suppress sin-I do not think the law should feel called upon to surround it with protection. And if the man indulges in the sin of illicit connection with a young girl, should the legislature feel particularly called upon to protect him from the possible consequence resulting from the fact of the youth of the girl concerned and protect him by really subjecting that girl to an imposition before a public court?
I must say that, supposing the result of that imposition was to establish that at some previous time or on some previous occasion she had forgotten herself, I do not see that it would be a very serious mitigation of the offence of the man.

I see the justness of the remarks made by the minister. On the other hand he knows, as I do, that there are girls who, at the age of sixteen, are fully developed and look much older than they really are. Supposing a man goes into a house of ill-fame or a house of assignation and meets one of these girls and has illicit connection with her- commits a sin to use the words of my hon. friend-it would not be fair that such a man should be brought before the court and accused of carnally knowing a girl under the age of sixteen, when the girl was not of chaste character previously but was known to be a prostitute. It is not fair, under such circumstances that that man should be held up before the law and found guilty of a crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not quite sure that even if a woman be a prostitute there is not such a public interest in preventing young girls being polluted under the age of sixteen as to justify making it an offence for any man who contributes towards the making of young girls prostitutes who are below that age. That is the case with the man which the hon. member places before us.
No, he finds her there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, if he and men like him did not go to houses of prostitution, or if they drew the line at girls under
sixteen, there would not be the encouragement to those girls to resort to that unfortunate profession, if I may so call it.

How is he going to
know if she looks like a girl of twenty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is fair for him to take his responsibility. He can satisfy himself.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 12-minimum sentence for stealing automobile:
What is the section that shall not apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that section 1035 would leave to the magistrate the discretion of imposing a fine. The other modification in the law affected by this section is to wipe out the maximum penalty. There was a maximum penalty of two years' and a minimum of one year's imprisonment. There did not seem to be any very good reason why a man stealing an automobile should get a lighter punishment than he was liable to get for the theft of some other article.
Why such active sympathy for the owners of automobiles?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all.
We declare the sentence for stealing an automobile shall not be less than one year's imprisonment. There does not seem to be any money penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This amendment is not introduced because of sympathy for automobile owners, but we have had brought home to us in the strongest possible way that the stealing of automobiles is exceedingly prevalent, and there is therefore greater cause for energetic measures to suppress crime that is prevalent than perhaps may be necessary in the case of offences that are of rare occurrence.
I suppose the committee will see that I am not the owner of an automobile.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Neither am I.

Why not make the offence similar for those who steal a horse and buggy? We know cases of young men who steal an automobile for a joy ride, and the automobile is either brought back or left by the roadside. A magistrate may decide that as a case of ordinary theft and the young men will be sent down for one year without the option of a fine. The

latter portion of the section says that the sentence shall not be suspended without the concurrence of the Attorney General. Why should we interfere with the judge in the discharge of his duty to take into consideration the circumstances in each particular case? Surely we ought to have confidence in our judiciary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the law as it
stands the judge has indefinite discretion to suspend. There are numerous other cases where he is not empowered to suspend sentence without the assent of the Attorney General. With regard to the question of the hon. member, why not make the penalty similar for the theft of a horse and buggy? -I have no reason to give except that I have already indicated, that there appears to be a special necessity to impress upon a large class of people who look upon the automobile as fair game the seriousness of what they are doing. I think it is generally recognized that one of the things you must consider in determining the degree of severity of punishment is the greater or less necessity for repression of the crime as evidenced by the greater or less prevalence of that crime.

Why should not the judge be given discretion in districts where the offence is not prevalent? If, for instance, in Toronto or Montreal, automobile stealing is prevalent, then the judge recognizing that fact sees that a heavy penalty is imposed. But take, for instance, the district of Three Rivers, where no such thing as theft is known-and some person falls from grace, a stranger to that district, the same sentence ought not to be meted out to the offender as would be the case in a district where the offence has become prevalent. I urge upon the committee that the courts should be given discretion to deal with these cases as in the past.

I think we all ought to be in sympathy with the object which this Bill hopes to attain, but personally I do not think it is wise to enact legislation which is going to facilitate the branding of people as jail-birds. It is a serious thing for a man to be put in jail- more serious probably than many of us realize; and when you make the crime of stealing an automobile such that there is no option but for the accused to serve a term in jail, I think the sentence is altogether out of proportion to the crime. If he is there for only a week, he and his children are branded for the rest of their natural 
lives as jail-birds. I endorse the sentiment of the last speaker (Mr. Jacobs) that some discretion surely ought to be left to the judge in these cases.

I think the remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka are quite in point, taken in connection with the fact that a great number of these automobile thefts are committed innocently. I do not think we should limit the discretion of a judge to consider favourable circumstances in the case of a boy who goes out for a joy-ride with somebody else's automobile. That is theft undoubtedly, and under this amendment he cannot escape with less than a year's imprisonment. I think the minister would be well advised to reconsider the section.

I have not a great deal of sympathy with the boy who takes an automobile and drives off with it! We have had those cases in Toronto. For the first year the magistrates treated them merely as joy-rides and let the boys off; from that the boys graduated to stealing cars, and finally they graduated into these bandits who are driving about the country shooting and robbing people. There have been half a dozen of these serious cases lately, and if you look up the records of the youths involved, some of whom have been sentenced to be hanged, you will find they were up before the magistrates in the first place on the charge of stealing automobiles for joyrides. At first the magistrates and judges were all inclined to think that taking a man's automobile from in front of his house or store was like borrowing his garden rake or hose, but when somebody suggested that while the car was borrowed the borrower * was using up the gasoline, and therefore stealing it, a conviction was obtained for the theft of the gasoline. Hardly a night passes in Toronto without there being four or five cars stolen. Cars are taken off by men who use them in connection with their operations in burglarizing banks and robbing the tills in the stores of merchants in small towns. The only way to stop a wave of crime of that kind is by drastic legislation. A nice little joy-ride is very often the first step toward a criminal career. A young fellow may take a car out, drive around in it for a while and then leave it where he got it; the owner comes out and wonders what is the matter with it. Then the next time a young fellow takes a car he gets drunk, perhaps, and smashes it. And all this time the law is saying to this fellow: Oh, you are all

right, we will not touch you. The gang of thugs that have been terrorizing Ontario is made up of boys some of whom are hardly out of their teens; and these fellows have been stealing automobiles for five or six years. A law of this kind will teach these people that they must leave motor cars alone, and you will find that much of this crime will cease.

It seems to me that the penalties provided by this clause are not too severe. If it is established that the accused is guilty, sentence may be suspended as provided by the Act. The new section says that sentence shall not be suspended without the concurrence of the Attorney General or his agent or of the counsel acting for the Crown in the prosecution of the offender. That means, however, that if the judge has the consent of the Attorney General or his agent he may suspend sentence. The case will be carefully examined, and if it is evident that the sentence should be suspended, the accused can be given fair play. It will be ascertained whether or not the automobile was taken as a joke; everything in favour of the man will be examined into. As the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has contended, the proposed amendment is not too severe. There are too many cases of stealing automobiles, and we must try to put a stop to it. I am in favour of this law; it is only just.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I may point out to
the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) that if he got just such a case as he supposes then we would have section 285B to deal with. If it was established that the act was a mere boyish freak, the judge would have absolute discretion to go as low as he liked in the way of punishment.

As a
matter of fact it is theft though, according to the definition of theft in the Code, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We must read the
definition of theft, but we must read also the section dealing with special cases. I think it is generally recognized that a disposition dealing with a special case makes an exception to a general disposition. Section 285B says:
Everyone who takes or causes to be taken from a garage, stable, stand or other building or place, any automobile or motor car with intent to operate or drive or use or cause or permit the same to be operated or driven or used without the consent of the owner shall be liable, on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding $500 and costs or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding twelve months or to both fine and imprisonment.
I do not think, therefore, that there is any danger that the really harmless boy will get harshly treated under this law.
I may point out that just the other day we were passing on a murder case in connection with which the first operation was the perfectly harmless thing that the hon. gentleman speaks of-the borrowing of somebody else's automobile for the purpose.
I simply mention this more recent case; we have had several such instances. The borrowed automobile is becoming one of the tools of trade of the burglar and the holdup artist. I hope hon. gentlemen will not allow themselves to be carried away with the sympathetic appeal of the odd case of a boy who may perhaps by mistake be convicted of stealing but who always has the opportunity of appealing to a very lenient and clement Solicitor General and Minister of Justice. I hope hon. gentlemen will not do that and forget the importance of impressing on the criminal population the seriousness of the offence of really stealing an automobile.
Are the offenders any more liable to be caught under the penalty provided in this Bill than under the present penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think they are more liable to be caught. But the whole theory of the criminal law is that it deters people from committing offences by providing penalties and punishments.
It is the certainty of the punishment rather than the extent of it which deters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The certainty is of
great importance, and we strive as far as possible to get it. But if you have certainty of punishment and the punishment itself is inadequate, you do not get very much effect. There is no disposition that we can put in this statute that will make it certain that the criminal will get caught; that we have to leave to the vigilance of those who are charged with the enforcement of law.

If I were satisfied that the minister's interpretation of the law was correct, I would not object to the clause as it stands. I have a distinct recollection of prosecuting in a somewhat similar case under a section placed some time ago in the Criminal Code; perhaps the minister will remember it. I can-

not quote it exactly at the moment, but it refers to the keeping of stray animals. I raised the contention in that case that it was theft. The judge before whom I was acting, and who, I think, was one of the brightest judges we have ever had in Canada, expressed himself as absolutely clear that it was theft and that the man could be prosecuted for theft, notwithstanding that in this other section it is dealt with in another way. This is a repetition of what I have suggested. This judge may be wrong and the minister may be right; but I have grave doubt whether my right hon. friend is right, and, therefore, I do not like the clause as it stands. I believe, that strictly according to law, that boy could be prosecuted under this section, and he must be sentenced for one year unless th6 Crown prosecutor or the Attorney General agrees. I suppose it is likely that where a case is such as I have mentioned, the Crown prosecutor or the Attorney General would agree.

Not agree, but
recommend.
Concurrence.
As long as there is concurrence, that is all that is required.

Once a man is
found guilty, the judge has no right to suspend sentence, but he has a right to consult with the Crown prosecutor or agent of the Crown, and then if the case is a fair one, the Crown prosecutor or agent of the Crown will recommend suspension of the sentence. The law is perfectly correct.

The hon. member (Mr. Thomson) is assimilating the crime of stealing an automobile with that of stealing a horse and buggy. There is all the difference in the world between the two. There are regular organizations of automobile thieves. They have places where they can take a car, run it into a garage, take the number off the engine, stamp on another number and get the car away to the United States. I had a case of a stolen car, and that car was found six months afterwards in a garage in New York where demonstrations were being made for technical schools. Automobile stealing is an organized trade, the same as that of counterfeiting. Insurance companies which insure automobiles against theft will tell you that it is the best organized system of robbery there is on the con-
[Mr. Thomson.
tinent. It is spreading all the time. Another thing which my hon. friend forgets is that a man who steals an automobile is not going to loaf around the street corners; he goes full speed with it, and he may kill any one on the road. Therefore, by trying to stop this automobile stealing business, you are protecting human life. I am not in favour of too drastic measures, but this is an evil that is spreading. In the city of Three Rivers, I must say that automobile theft has come to be a fashion, not that the people of that city steal automobiles, but we have visits from people from Montreal. There have been automobiles stolen in Three Rivers, a distance of 96 miles from Montreal, and on a telephone message being sent to Montreal, two hours afterwards the automobile was traced in that city. That shows the danger to which men, women, children, horses and so on are exposed on the road between Three Rivers and Montreal. This is an evil that ought to be stamped out. If judges are too kind-hearted, we might bring in the Attorney General or his representatives, of whom we have two worthy ones in this House, and we have had an expression of views from one who, for a number of years, has been a representative of the Attorney General in Montreal. We can trust such officials as they are to see that justice is meted out and that no injustice is done. May I add for the information of the hon. gentleman, that in the Criminal Code there is a provision that for stealing a cow a man is liable to go to penitentiary for fourteen years?
Not to exceed fourteen years. [DOT]
I know that, and he cannot run away with a steer so fast as to endanger the life of people along the road very much.

Coming from a city of the size of Hamilton in which automobile stealing is prevalent, I would be neglecting my duty if I did not say a word or two in regard to this legislation. We have a provision now by which those who steal automobiles may be hauled up and fined, and sent to jail if they do not pay the fine. There is five times as much stealing of automobiles as there was a year ago, and this crime is increasing very rapidly. I have an automobile which I keep in a good barn at the back of my house. I have had the panels pulled out of the door twice while I have been in bed

and the police have chased the thieves away. It is pretty nearly impossible to keep a $5,000 or $6,000 automobile without scalawags trying to break in one's doors to get it away. It is absolutely necessary that something should be done to stop these people from doing that sort of thing. We are neglecting our duty if we do not change the law, and I think that if the law provided that automobile thieves could be lashed, we would put more terror into them.

This is a very bad
clause. I have no objection to the penalty being increased if the law is not severe enough; but to pass a statute which says that a judge, no matter what the circumstances may be, shall not have within himself the right to suspend sentence or to give a sentence of less than a year, seems to me a serious reflection upon the judiciary of the country.
A judge in certain cases must sentence a man to be hanged.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In cases of stealing
from the post office or the mails, a judge has to give not less than three years.

Probably the same
argument which I make here would apply to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is not a solitary case.	,

That would not affect my argument, which is that you will not deter people from crime by providing heavy penalties. When there was, on the statute books of the Old Country and probably of this country, the death penalty for half a dozen or a dozen crimes, there was more crime than there is now. When a man could be hanged for sheep-stealing, sheep-stealing was more common than it is to-day. It is not the severity of the penalty; it is the certainty of the penalty that is required. This is a move in the wrong direction. Let people who steal automobiles be punished as severely as the judge with whom the application of the law is left deems best, but do not tie the judge's hands in a case which may easily come up where a light sentence should be imposed. Let me give a specific instance, an imaginary case, a hypothetical case.
Keep to the old word "imaginary."

All right, I will imagine this case. A young man, the only
support of a widowed mother, steals a car. He just wants a joy-ride. He is caught. He repents. He is really sorry.
Oh, oh.

People repent sometimes and are really sorry. A judge, convinced that the young man is really sorry, might think it wise to impose a penalty much lighter than a year's imprisonment, but under this provision his hands are tied unless he gets the consent of the Crown prosecutor. I believe this clause is a mistake and that it will not have the desired effect.

The hon. member for
Brome (Mr. McMaster) touched the very point when he said' that what is required in the law is the certainty of the penalty. That is what we are providing here. I have in my mind at the moment, magistrates who for months and years would not fine because they would never get into an automobile themselves; they looked upon them as gewgaws, something outrageous, that people should not have-they themselves would rather walk to the court. If an automobile got smashed up, that was all right; it was something that was not necessary in the first place, according to these magistrates. Now we must prevent the idiosyncrasies of the judges from interfering with the penalty in this way. We must have a fixed penalty, and that is what the law is providing. I think the law is a good one, and the hon. member who has just sat down has given us the very reason why we should pass the section.

I have always been very much opposed to this idea of leaving it in the power of the judge to pass a sentence with his right hand, and to suspend that sentence with his left. I know of a case right down in my own part of the country, in the constituency of my hon. friend across the harbour, the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), where a young man was walking abroad in the streets of North Sydney with four suspended sentences upon his shoulders at the one time. One sentence was for stealing an automobile, another was for shooting his own brother through the lungs so severely that four doctors were required to save him. In spite of the four sentences that were on his shoulders at the one time, he was walking abroad just the same as any law-abiding citizen.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: What were the other two sentences?

Perhaps I had better not mention them, but if my hon. friend wants to know, the third sentence was for an attempt to commit rape. In spite of his four sentences, politics kept this young man walking the street.
Shame!

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-persons under 21 and guilty of theft liable to be spanked:

I should like to have
from the minister his definition of the word " spanked " before we go any further.
My hon. friend ought to remember what happened to him in his youth.
It is so long ago that I have forgotten.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry my hon.
friend's memory is so short. My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce or myself might be excused if we had forgotten, but not a young man like my hon. friend. The hon. member will find the information he wants on page 10. It is as follows:
(1)	Whenever spanking may he awarded for any offence the court may sentence the offender to he once, twice or thrice spanked within the limits of the prison, under the supervision of the medical officer of the prison, or if there be no such officer, or if the medical officer he for any reason unable to be present, then, under the supervision of a surgeon or physician to be named by the Minister of Justice in the case of prisons under the control of the Dominion, and in the case of other prisons by the attorney general of the province in which such prison is situated.
(2)	The number of the strokes shall be specified in the sentence; 1 the offender shall be spanked upon the bare buttocks; and the instrument to be used shall be a leather strap [DOT]not longer than eighteen inches or wider than two and one-half inches or narrower than one inch or thicker than one-quarter of an inch.
(3)	No female shall be spanked.

Now that women have
the vote, I do not see why they should be deprived of this privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the bon. member
chooses to move an amendment we shall be pleased to consider it.
I would like my hon. friend to cut that 'ection out and keep it in his vest pocket.

I had understood that spanking was slapping with the open hand,

but I find by the dictionary that to spank is:
to strut, to stalk; comp. Sc. Spang, to leap.

That is French.
Mr. BUREAU (reading!:
to move with a quick lively step:
That is not French. It may he Irish: to slap .or smack, as with the open hand.
The latter is what I understood spanking to mean, but it seems that we are going to go back to the Middle Ages and use leather straps of a certain width and length on the bare buttocks. That is something that I thought pertained only to animals, so I took the trouble to look it up in the dictionary, and I find this:
Buttock, the rump, or the protuberant part of an animal behind.
I did not know that by legislation we were seeking to consecrate the protuberant part of an animal behind to human beings. But, leaving aside the dictionary definition, Mr. Chairman, I think it is ridiculous legislation to provide that a hoy of twenty, who is pretty well grown, and very often well developed, should be put across a man's knees and spanked. I do not think we ought to put such legislation upon our statute books. It is taking us back to the Middle Ages. We might just as well erect stocks in our public squares and have people fastened down to them to be insulted by every passer-by. I think it is ridiculous legislation. I am in favour of whipping for rape. I think that is the greatest crime; I think it is much worse than murder for a man to take hold of an innocent girl and assault her; I am in favour of whipping for that offence, hut not for theft. In England in the old days they used to hang a man for stealing a sheep. We do not want to go back to those days, but here we are starting to spank boys of nineteen and twenty years of age for theft. I say that we might just as well go hack to the instruments of tortue in the olden days. I am opposed to this section. I do not say that it was inspired by hysterical persons, as my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) has suggested, but it is certainly hysterical legislation.

If we pass legislation
dealing with the rump, we shall be under the imputation, it seems to me, of being a Rump Parliament. This is what we might call the Joker in the entire Bill as presented by the minister. I think it is beneath

the dignity of Parliament to declare that people up to twenty-one years of age shall be spanked. We have had in this Parliament men twenty-one years of age, and under this section they would be liable to be taken out and spanked.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps they deserved it.

I have not had the long parliamentary experience that my hon. friend has had. The definition of "spank" in the dictionary I have before me is this:
To strike with the open hand, as to spank a small hoy.
That is practically what it is. We have all of us had spanking in our early days-some of us not as often as we should have had perhaps, on the principle that if you spare the rod you spoil the child-but I cannot understand how a rule of this kind, inserted in our criminal law, is going to help the situation. If a boy is guilty of stealing, he ought to be dealt with as a thief. The younger boy under sixteen is sent to the reformatory under the Juvenile Delinquents Act. We have a system in our law whereby children under a certain age may not be tried in public, but in private by a Juvenile Delinquents Court judge, and they are thus removed from the bad influences of police or general criminal courts where older offenders are tried. It is the tendency of newer legislation to bring these children up by kindly methods, and to make them see the error of their ways, treating them generally in such a way that their outlook upon the world will be of an honest and kindly nature. But to take a boy to prison, and give some person other than his father or mother the right to punish him by applying the rod in a prison yard, seems to me, as my hon. friend from three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) says, to be going back to the old days. We should change our views in the matter of penalties to be imposed upon criminals, particularly young boys, and I for one am not in favour of this legislation. I should be inclined to ask the committee to strike it out.

I would suggest
that the punishment be made applicable to the second, instead of the first, offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I say, in response to hon. gentlemen who talk about going back to ancient days-

The Middle Ages.
248i
They may be flogging returned soldiers at that rate, for some unfortunate offence, if the age is fixed at 21. The thing is brutal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I had expected that if there was a fault to be found with this legislation, it would be as respects the novelty of the punishment for the offence. Punishment that involves nothing in the nature of keen physical suffering people have found very amusing, and a subject to be facetious about, and that is the great value of it. If you take the budding embryonic Jesse James, who is out to be a hero among his fellow youngsters, and send him to a reformatory or a gaol, to associate with criminals, and he comes back and tells his tale, he is a hero-
Ti-Noir Desjardins, for instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let us keep to the particular case-but if he comes back with the glorious story to tell, that he got a spanking, then he is not a hero among his companions; and I think that the real value of this punishment is that it takes the dignity out of the profession of crime. I have an estimate of the application, more or less legal, of the results of this sort of punishment in quite a number of cases, under the order of a judge who has dealt very largely with that class of criminals, and he has certified in the strongest terms that it is most effective.
Where is this spanking in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In Ontario; it has
been done, as I said, more or less legally.
Illegally.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, more or less
illegally, then; perhaps more illegally than legally. But what we are concerned with is its effect in dealing with juvenile delinquents. I do think it is a matter of first importance to make them realize, in their earlier years, that there is no glory to be got out of crime, and I think that the real value of this legislation is that it does put these children-and after all they are only children-in the position of being ridiculous in the eyes of their companions.
It brutalizes them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Brutalizes them? Why, I may say that in my school days boys were strapped, and I hope, at least, that we were not brutalized thereby.
There was good reason for it then.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, we are assuming, in the present case, that the punishment will be applied only when there is good reason. I do myself, in all earnestness, think that this would be a very useful adjunct to present methods of correction. It involves nothing that could brutalize any one, and afi.er all, it is a means of correction that has been applied from time immemorial to all the children of succeeding generations.
By the State, or State officials?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not necessarily by the State, or State officials, but it has been applied in the educational systems of different countries for long periods of years.
It has been abandoned by most countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Personally, I think it
is a question whether it was an improvement to give it up. At all events, however that may be, a punishment of this kind, which inflicts no real physical suffering of any gravity, but does bring the child to realize that he is being treated like a foolish child, and not like an heroic defier of the laws of society, would be a really great advantage, and in addition I have the testimony of the results of its application, coming from a judge for whose opinion I have great respect. I submit the clause to the consideration of thq committee. For myself personally I believe it to be a good clause, and one that sooner or later, when this committee has got more accustomed to the proposal and has thought it over a little more quietly, will come to be the law of the country, to its great advantage. I am not disposed to insist upon it if the committee thinks that it comes too suddenly and is not prepared just yet to pass it; nor shall I insist on maintaining the age fixed at 21. If it would make it more acceptable, I would fix the age at 18, at which children may be treated under the Juvenile Delinquents Act.

The minister knows very
well that we are adopting now, in the treatment of juvenile delinquents, a method of kindly treatment. He knows that we try to make them realize that they are of some use in this world even though they may have fallen, and that there is an opportunity for them to rise. Contrast that with this system of half-flogging, taking a young boy into the prison yard and having the sentence inflicted by the

gaoler or some person under his instructions. It is a most brutal suggestion, and I am surprised that a kindly-hearted man like the Minister of Justice should promote legislation of this kind in this House.

For the last fifteen or
sixteen years I have had a good many cases to defend in the Juvenile Courts. As the minister has said, there have been cases of this kind of treatment imposed upon young prisoners in the province of Ontario, usually, I think, with the consent of the father, the consent being obtained by the magistrate insisting that it be given. There is a precedent for this, as the minister has suggested. I think that probably this follows the old system of whipping at the cart's tail; and there was another method adopted at the same time for the same class of offence, that of standing the prisoner in the pillory, and putting a split stick on his tongue until sunset. And this is just about in the same class as that legislation. Now, I submit that it is a dangerous thing-particularly with a first offender-that a young boy, perhaps a timid, frail, nervous youngster, should be slugged by some big burly policeman with his belt and buckle, and everything that is attached to it, while the rest of the policemen stand around and view the exhibition. I think it is something we should not do. It does not seem to be fair and just, in view of the public feeling that has been aroused and has culminated in a sentiment as a result of which boys are now treated in a different way. Even if formerly a ball and chain was attached to their ankles, nowadays they are given the benefit, if it is at all possible, in the case of first offenders, of a suspended sentence; then afterwards if it is shown that the efforts to save them have been fruitless a more rigorous treatment is carried out. I for one, after some fifteen or sixteen years of criminal practice, such as you would have in an Ontario city, must say that I think this legislation is being asked for chiefly by the Chief Constables Association of Canada. We have heard it advocated, and I am altogether opposed to it. I think public opinion is opposed to such treatment, particularly in the case of a first offender. It appears to me that we are descending to a point that cannot be justified in view of what the people think at the present time. The effort should be made to make the young boy better, instead of humiliating him and making him feel discouraged, and that he has nothing to live for. Because he will feel that way after

an ordeal such as this, which is half-brother to the cat-o'-nine-tails system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would have no objection to limit the clause to second offences and reduce the age to eighteen. Nevertheless I do not at all share the view that there is anything inhuman, or anything cruel, or anything brutalising in this punishment. I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman who has just sat down that he has given a very unfair description of what is proposed to be done. The section specially provides to make impossible such conduct on the part of the "brutal constable" with his "belt and buckle," and all the rest, surrounded by other brutal policemen.

The constable will wield
the strap.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He will wield the strap but he will do it under the supervision of qualified physicians named precisely 'for the purpose. Every protection will be taken to see there is no brutality. I am quite willing to admit that there is argument to be made against this proposition, but it is beyond me to realize how arguments can be based upon the suggestion of brutality. That, I think, is carrying the thing very much too far. There is room for difference of opinion, that I am prepared to concede. However, I am not disposed to insist on passing this legislation at the present time, because it is a new proposal; but I have confidence that when people will have given a little reflection to it,-and eliminated from their minds the effect of the pictures we have had to-day of a condition of affairs that will never exist under the law if it is passed-it will have a better reception. Under the circumstances I beg to withdraw the clause, and that also involves the withdrawal of clause 28.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, clauses 13 and 28 withdrawn.
On section 14-marks used on public stores.
What is the affect of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are in the
section a number of marks indicating the property of the Militia Department or other departments. The marks "P. W.", for example, indicate the property of the Public Works Department.
Why should the marks cn public property be a matter that must be dealt with in the Criminal Code?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is for the purpose of enabling them to be identified. The legal affect of the section in question has not been modified in the slightest degree. There is only one additional kind of mark. The provision is that the marks specified in this section in that behalf may be applied in, or on, any public works to denote His Majesty's property in such stores.
