There is a provision as to unlawfully applying these marks, a provision making it an offence to obliterate marks from public stores, and a provision making the unlawful possession, sale, and so forth, of public stores bearing these marks an offence. The effect of this is merely to give to the stores of the Public Works Department the same protection that the law already extends to Government property in connection with other departments.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15-three card monte, etc., forbidden.
I understand that this legislation is the result of a judgment handed down by a judge of our Court of Appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. It reproduces the provisions of a Bill introduced by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafor-tune) and deals with what is a growing evil to-day in the city of Montreal. As the result of a judgment of the courts, that under the law three card monte was not per se a gambling game, all the experts in three card monte have swarmed into Montreal and they are really pillaging the unsuspecting citizens of that town at a rate that is something appalling. I do hope -in order that I may be able to return home in safety with my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier and my hon. friend from Georges Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) - that the House will pass this section.
What would be included in the term "any similar game"? And who would decide?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The court will have to decide.

The provision against playing three card monte or inducing other people to play is all right, but adding the words "or any similar game," is, I think, rather dangerous and leaves it to the interpretation of any judge whatsoever. He would have to be a card expert, otherwise his decision would not be of much value.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the principle of three card monte consists in a sleight-of-hand trick which may be operated just as well with other things as with cards. I may say that I was under the necessity of calling upon a very distinguished member of this House to give me an illustration-
May we have his name, please?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
in order that I
might be inspired with a proper horror of the game. As I understand, what is sought to be struck at is not only this particular game with cards, but any game on a similar principle which involves betting upon a guess which a man makes as to the result of some sleight-of-hand trick. I would not think that the court would find it very difficult to determine what under those circumstances was meant by a "similar game." It is absolutely impossible of achievement to try in advance to define all the possible ways by which that kind of swindle can be carried on.
Why does not the minister make the game criminal wherever it is played?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The supposition is, of course, absolutely impossible to entertain, but suppose my hon. friend and his neighbour and myself chose to sit down in the quiet of his home and fool away our time in guessing at each other's endeavours to place the cards here and there, I do not see what evil would come to the public. What we are trying to repress is the evil of playing this game in public places and so inducing others to participate. I may say that the provision was drafted by my hon. and learned friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafortune) who has had a long experience in the criminal courts and has had an opportunity of familiarising himself with this trouble in the city of Montreal. If we can make1 provision against the public carrying on this game we will have struck at an evil that calls for repression. We have no evidence that there is any need of interfering with private amusements.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-penalty of whipping for robbery and assault with intent to rob:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have had this particular provision urged on me from numerous quarters because the crime of robbery with violence is increasing with alarming rapid-

ity, and not infrequently it results in the death of the person sought to be robbed. It has been impressed upon me by authorities in different parts of the country that we should endeavour by every means to repress that particular form of crime. It has been pointed out, although I have not been able to verify the figures, that in the adjoining states where a similar law has been consistently applied good results have become apparent.

While I do not wish to
oppose this clause, I must express my disapproval of extending this severe punishment any further. I understand that under the law garroting is punishable by whipping, and I suppose robbery with violence may be considered a similar offence. I would point out to the minister that in the case of section 13, which was dropped, we were proposing to sentence young thieves to be whipped, and now under this section when they become older thieves they are to be flogged. Both sections seem to be steps in the same direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The youngsters were only to be spanked; these thieves are to be whipped.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-fraudulently burning any chattel over $25 in value:
What has occasioned the insertion of this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is at the request
of the Attorney General of Ontario, who points out that the crime of arson can only be committed with regard to the burning of something in the nature of real property. There does not seem to be any good reason why it should not be susceptible of being committed by the burning of chattels or movable things. I think the cases that specially brought it to his attention were the burning of automobiles.

Burning the mortgage
of a church when the debt is paid off, for instance.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 18

penalty for injuring, etc., oil well extended to gas wells:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is simply applying to-gas wells the section which already applies to oil wells.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 19-docking animals forbidden:

That is a most unusual
clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
These three sections,
19, 20 and 21, all have to do with cruelty to animals. They are introduced at the suggestion and very earnest request of the various societies for the prevention of cruelty to animals. They have been submitted to the careful consideration of the professional men in the Department of Agriculture and meet with their approval. It may further be said that their effect is in some measure to bring our provisions with regard to cruelty to animals up to date, if I may use the expression. At all events, these amendments put us on a level with the progress that has been made in recent years in Great Britain and in most of the other Dominions in regard to such legislation. I think any one examining our present provisions will find that they hardly come up to what in the judgment of the present day would constitute cruelty to animals. While I have spoken of these clauses as urged upon us by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, I may say that they do not by any means grant all that was asked. We have tried to avoid extremes and to content ourselves with putting our legislation on a footing of equality with the legislation prevailing in the countries to which I have referred.

I am surprised to learn that legislation of this kind has originated in Great Britain. I know it is a habit in England to have the tails of horses docked. I can understand that the provision may have been suggested by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, but I would point out that sometimes societies of that kind are not to be relied upon; they often allow their hearts to run away with their heads. Is the minister in a position, to say when this law was introduced in Great Britain?
Would this provision interfere with the docking of lambs' tails, an operation which is carried on in the spring on pretty nearly every farm in the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I find that the animals to which the present provision of the Act applies are "any dog, bird, beast or other animal, not being cattle", etc. In the definition of "cattle" I find that the term includes "any horse, mule, ass, swine, sheep or goat," and so on. Apparently "cattle" does include "horse;" therefore, as cattle are excluded from this section, it would not apply to horses.

Then horses may be
docked under this new legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no prohibition.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 22-metal tokens used as money forbidden.
What is the meaning of this provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand the purpose is this: the existing sections had the effect of prohibiting the issuing of coins having a money value or redeemable in money. This is to extend it to the issuance of coins redeemable in goods.
Has any abuse existed which makes it necessary to have new legislation on this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The legislation is asked for by the Finance Department. I fancy they must have found necessity for it in connection with their dealing with the question of coinage generally.

It seems to me that part of this clause is rather confusing and hard to understand. It says:
Provided, however, that such intent shall not be necessary to constitute such offence in case such coin or token is made or issued with the intention (the disproof whereof shall lie on the accused) of entitling the holder thereof-
Meaning, I assume, the person who is disposing of the false token.
-to receive therefor, to the extent of the value denoted thereon, goods or merchandise from the person so charged as aforesaid.
Well, suppose that the person parted with a false token denominated in value $5 and got half that value in goods, the crime would still be there but it is not provided for. If I understand the clause aright, before a crime could be committed, one would need to have the exact value of the goods represented by the token. I should like the minister to say whether or not the section would not be abortive without some further amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not be quite
disposed to agree with the hon. gentleman's interpretation. If a coin, or certificate, or any document entitles me to obtain "to the extent of", that puts a limit to what I can possibly obtain, but within that limit I may obtain by it anything less. As regards the words:
Of entitling the holder thereof to receive therefor, to the extent of the value-
The question is not what he actually gets ultimately; the question is whether

this is a coin which entitles "the holder thereof to receive therefor, to the extent of the value denoted thereon, goods or merchandise." It will not be affected by the question whether he gets goods or merchandise to the whole amount. If the coin itself entitles him to get goods to the extent of $5, then the issuing of it is an offence without regard to whether he succeeds or not in getting that amount.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 23-reading deposition on preliminary inquiry.

What change is made by
the proposed new section 684? It seems to be our law at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The new portion of the first subsection consists of the words:
If the evidence has not been taken in shorthand-
Section 684, as at present, applies the same rule without distinction whether evidence has been taken in shorthand or not. This amendment makes the rule applicable only when evidence has not been taken in shorthand. This is to obviate the inconvenience, when evidence is taken in shorthand, of reading over from the shorthand notes all that has been said. It is to be remembered that we are dealing with a case of evidence taken in the presence of the accused.
When evidence is taken in shorthand before the courts in Montreal the case is enlarged for two, three or four days until the evidence is written out. Then the prisoner is asked to plead.

Where a preliminary
investigation is taken, either by a judge himself or by some one else in longhand, the depositions can be signed and the judge can give his decision immediately. When the depositions are taken in shorthand, they have to be transcribed and signed, according to the law, before the judge decides whether there is ground or not for trial, whereas, now, according to this amendment, the decision can be given immediately before the notes are transcribed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand the reading over which is in contemplation is the reading over which would take place when a man is called upon to say whether he has anything to say.
The evidence is not read over when it is taken in shorthand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The effect of this will be to dispense with the necessity of reading

over the evidence where it has been taken in shorthand.

The second part of the
section does not seem to change in any way whatever the old rule with regard to the words to be addressed to the prisoner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only reason for
the second subsection being inserted, as I understand the matter, is that it has come to be the practice, when you amend a section, to repeal the whole section and to substitute the amending section. There is some trifling alteration, I am informed.

What is the change
in the first subsection? It looks like the old law to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have inserted in
the subsection the words "when the evidence has not been taken in shorthand." Under the existing provision, whether evidence was taken in shorthand or longhand, it is required that before the prisoner is called upon to plead, the evidence shall be read over to him. There is a purpose in that reading over where the evidence is taken, not in shorthand, but in longhand, because I understand then the prisoner is called upon to sign the deposition.

He is asked "having
heard the evidence", and he has not heard the evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He has sat in court
and has heard the evidence.
When he has sat there, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When evidence is taken in shorthand, it is quite impossible that he should be asked to sign the shorthand * notes.
The law provides now that he need not sign if the evidence is taken in shorthand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then, what is the
purpose of reading it all over to him? He has sat there and listened to it all. This is simply, as I understand it, to obviate the necessity of going through an operation that produces no useful results.
What is the law now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The law now is, that whether the evidence be taken in shorthand or longhand, it must be read over, unless with the consent of the accused.

In my experience, I have never met with any difficulty at all. We always got along splendidly. The notes

were taken down in shorthand, and there seemed to be no trouble about the matter. Perhaps we took too much tor granted in not requiring the reading over of the evidence when taken in shorthand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Unfortunately, the
law as it stands requires that. Perhaps it is observed in some places and, perhaps, in others people, seeing the futility of the law, do not try to observe it. 1 confess I am not familiar with the proceedings In the particular situation that is in question. My learned friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) who has, I think, considerable experience in the carrying on of criminal cases, and my learned friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Lafortune) who also occupies the same position, might be able to put more clearly before the committee just what happens. What I understand to be the purpose of this modification was to produce this result: whereas at present, whether taken in shorthand or in longhand the evidence has to be read over if you want to comply with the letter of the law-
Is it not to avoid the trouble of a motion being made because the evidence had not been read over?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because the shorthand notes were not read over to the prisoner.
This only applies to depositions taken in longhand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provision is that the magistrate without regard as to how the evidence is taken down, shall ask the * prisoner whether he wishes the depositions to be read, and unless the accused dispenses therewith, he shall read or cause them to be read again. Where the evidence has been taken in shorthand, the magistrate now has to do that. The effect of this amendment will be to reduce the application of the section to cases where the evidence has been taken in longhand.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 25-prosecution for officers stealing fares to be tried summarily only with consent of accused.
What officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Conductors, and so forth, stealing fares.

"Officials" is what is
meant?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Officials is probably the word that was intended. We had last year a special provision made for dealing
with this offence of stealing fares, which formerly used to be dealt with under the statute which deals with receiving secret commissions. It was found that applying that law gave rise to great difficulty, and it was thought better to deal specifically with the offence of stealing fares. In dealing with it, a provision was made under which there might be a summary proceeding, but no provision was made as to who was to have the option as to whether the case should be summarily proceeded with. The purpose of this section is to give the option to the accused, which seems to be right.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 26-conviction of keeper prima facie evidence of premises being a disorderly house.

I am against this new rule being inserted in our legislation. I thought the old British rule was that a person is innocent until he is proven guilty. Here we are providing that it is only necessary to say that on one previous occasion the party was guilty, to give prima facie evidence that he is guilty a second time. That is a wide departure from the rule in criminal law, except in some special and particular cases. I should like to know why this new rule is sought to be introduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman has exactly seized the purpose of the clause. The effect of the clause is that where a party who is keeping a particular house is convicted of being the keeper of a disorderly house, that house will prima facie be presumed to be a disorderly house. We want to avoid this somewhat anomalous condition, where prosecutions are directed against one person for keeping a disorderly house, and against another person for being an inmate of that disorderly house. Surely when it has once been established on the conviction of the keeper that she is the keeper of a disorderly house, it does not seem an unfair thing that you should not have to begin all over again, when you start to prosecute a frequenter of that house, to prove that it is a disorderly house. There might be some exception if you were making it conclusive proof, but we are only making it prima facie evidence, leaving it to the frequenter to disprove, if he can, that it is a disorderly house.
It is contrary to the principle of our criminal law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Our criminal law
creates a good many exceptions from the principle, and this seems to be a very rational one.

The minister knows, I suppose, that frequently these houses are found to be such by the magistrate on character evidence alone, without any specific act ever being proven. That makes it very dangerous for persons who may be ignorant of the character of the house-for boarders or lodgers, for instance. Of course, it is a different matter with persons who are not there innocently. Convictions have been made right along -I think this is one of the cases where there is no election-on the evidence of a policeman, or perhaps two policemen, as to the reputation of the house. Upon that evidence the magistrate will impose a penalty, and give the house that reputation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This section does not affect the question of whether a person may or may not be innocently in a disorderly house. I do not understand that it would affect any right that now exists in a person found in a disorderly house to establish his ignorance or anything else which may justify him. This is limited exclusively to the question whether that is a disorderly house, and the effect of the enactment is to say that when it is once decided that that house is a disorderly house, then, when you have occasion to prove that with regard to some other individual than the one in whose case that question was decided, you will start with the prima facie idea that what was decided against the keeper of the house was well decided, and you will not have to begin all over again to prove in the case of a frequenter or inmate that it was a disorderly house. I would say that this was a very objectionable provision if it were to the effect that the conviction shall be conclusive evidence that it is a disorderly house, but it is only prima facie evidence. It is only a question of throwing the burden of proof on the party found in the house that has just been decided to be a disorderly house. The frequenter may rebut that, if he can. The cases in which this question arises are very numerous. A woman is arrested for keeping a disorderly house, and half a dozen girls and men are also arrested for being inmates of a disorderly house, the house being one and the same house. What happens is that you proceed to try the 
keeper, and it is absolutely essential to the conviction of the keeper that it should be decided that that is a disorderly house.
It is open to the accused to prove the contrary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. All that this does is. to dispense with the prosecutor who has got a judgment that it is a disorderly house from beginning all over again to prove that it is a disorderly house when the case of an inmate or frequenter comes before him, and it leaves it perfectly open to the accused to disprove that it is a disorderly house, or to establish his ignorance, lack of knowledge, or anything else. That is all the effect it has.

But we are dealing with the disorderly house itself. My objection is that this reverses all the principles of our law, and I do not see why we should go out of our way in this particular case to do any such thing as that. We ought to consider these rules of law as sacred. They have stood the test of hundreds of years, and we should make no change now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This section says that when it has been proved that the house is a disorderly house, it will not be necessary to begin all over again and establish the fact once more. What universal principles that is overriding I must confess I am at a loss to know.
It shifts the burden of proof to the other side.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When the Court has then and there decided that there is sufficient evidence that the house is a disorderly house, it is provided here that the Court will not have to begin over again, hear all the same evidence, and decide once more that the house is disorderly. But We say to any second person who is to be tried that if there is anything which he can put forward to rebutt that evidence upon which the Court has just found that it was a disorderly house, he can bring it forward and it will be heard. It Is only a question of saving a useless repetition.
Sometimes these seemingly "useless repetitions" are very valuable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And sometimes a too rigid adherence to general principles involves hardship.

The objection I see to the section is this. A frequenter may be tried at one time, the person charged with

keeping a disorderly house having been tried the week before. The person charged as a frequenter may have had no knowledge whatever of the previous prosecution, And when he or she is brought up a week later to answer the charge of being a frequenter of the house, without any knowledge whatever of the former proceedings, there is thrown upon that person the burden of proving that the place in which he or she had been was not a disorderly house. The offences and the persons charged being different, there is a possibility that the hearings may be entirely separate, and a man charged with being a frequenter might have no knowledge whatever of what had taken place in connection with the prosecution for the keeping of the disorderly house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is force in what the hon. gentleman points out. I do not think it turns so much on the point of different dates of trial, as on the question of the time at which the offence is charged as having been committed. I move to amend the section by adding at the end thereof the words:
As against any person charged with being or having been an inmate or frequenter of such house.
That is the case that is sought to be got at.

I do not think that this provision should be enacted, be-
5 p.m. cause you might have separate trials.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The trials may be separate, but the amendment applies to offences that are all committed at the same time. I do not refer to the time of trial but to the time at which it is charged the offence was committed.

I do not agree with the amendment, because a person charged with keeping a disorderly house may have been convicted so often that he or she is ready to plead guilty and pay the fine. Such a person might not be keeping a disorderly house at all, but possibly might want to have some other person convicted of being an inmate of a disorderly house and so would plead guilty to the offence, and the person charged with being a frequenter is not entitled to take any part in the proceedings against the person charged with keeping the disorderly house. He is not a party to the prosecution; he cannot open his mouth, or direct the course of the trial; and the evidence upon which the fact of
keeping the disorderly house is established may be flimsy in the extreme. But the person charged with keeping the disorderly house will plead guilty, and then the alleged frequenter is bound by the evidence in those proceedings; whereas, if he were a party to the prosecution, he might be able to set up facts which would entirely disprove, at the time of the prosecution for keeping the house, that it was a disorderly house at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would agree with
the hon. member, if we were holding the party who is charged as an inmate as being absolutely bound by the finding of the court. But we are not proposing to do that. We are leaving it absolutely open to him to submit every proof that he might have given had he been a party to the first trial. We are closing no door upon him at all. We are merely saying that we will not require the prosecution to bring again all the evidence upon which the court at that previous trial established that the house was a disorderly one. I think that any one who has had occasion to know anything about prosecutions for offences in connection with disorderly houses realizes that it is one class of offence that is surrounded with the greatest possible difficulty of proving the facts. I have not had much to do with that class of case, but I have had occasion to be present in court, when everything made it absolutely obvious that the house was a disorderly one, you had only to look at the people to know what kind of house they came out of, and yet there was great splitting of hairs before the court about the evidence as to whether the house was a disorderly house or not. And this is, not infrequently, in cases where a week before these same women and the same inmates, with regard to the same house, had been before the court, when all the evidence had been gone through and the court had then been satisfied that the house was a disorderly one. All that is sought now is to establish a prima facie presumption that will throw the burden of proof upon the people implicated. I hope that the amendment, worded in accordance with the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie), will be accepted, for I do not think it is objectionable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Doherty moves to amend section 26 by adding at the end thereof the following words:
As against any persbn charged with being or having been at the same time an inmate or frequenter of the said disorderly house.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: Who asked for this 'legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It came from the
people who have charge of prosecuting cases of this kind in the city of Montreal.

The Minister of Justice told me he intended to have that amendment applied only in cases where several people were arrested at the one time, and then if the proceedings at the first trial were against the proprietor and he was convicted of being the owner of a disorderly house, that conviction could he used against the other prisoners as being prima _ facie evidence that the House was a disorderly house. I may be mistaken but from my reading of the amendment it does not mean that. It means that the conviction could be used against any person charged with being an inmate of that house two months or six months afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that, subject to the criticism of my hon. friend the new wording I have drawn will make clear what we are all agreed we want to get. That is if we add to the clause the words:
as against any person charged with heing or having been at the same time-*
Now I think that can only refer back to the same time at which the keeper was found to be the keeper-

an inmate or frequenter of the said disorderly house.
I think what we want to get at is this. It is found that this woman was on July 15, the keeper of a disorderly house because she kept that disorderly house. If it be proved that John Jones on July 15 was in that house you do not need to prove again that it was a disorderly house. I think the words I have drawn mean that. If it can be made any more clear I shall be glad to accept any suggestion that will produce that result.

Although I hate to take up the time of the House, I ask a moment to suggest that it is a dangerous principle to introduce into the criminal law to take for granted that any trial, or any decision, at which the prisoner was not necessarily present, or to which the prisoner was not necessarily a party to, should be a basis for his conviction in a subsequent trial. I think the whole proceedings of his trial from the bottom up should take place in his presence. In this case we are taking for granted that some trial at which he was not present at all, and of which he did not necessarily have
[The Chairman. 1
any knowledge, shall be the basis for his conviction. I am entirely opposed to any system of criminal law, under which the whole business as to the man's criminality shall not be tried and threshed out once and for all in the presence of the prisoner.

Is there any very great
reason why this section should be put in? I thoroughly agree with what the hon member for North Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and the hon. member for Dorchestei (Mr. Cannon) have said. It appears tc me to be a most unfair phase of criminal law, if I may use the expression, that you should make a man liable for something he never had a chance to prove himself innocent of. Innumerable instances would arise where the whole thing may be proved to have been planned against some one for some particular purpose. The proceedings under which that man is found guilty of the offence may be conducted in his absence and the throwing upon him of the onus of proving his innocence is wrong in law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I point out it
is not said that the man is "prima facie" guilty. All that is said is that this house is a disorderly house. It still remains to be proved that he was there, and that he was there at the time at which the convicted person was found to be the keeper of such disorderly house. Frankly it does seem to me that the absolutely strict adherence to principle with regard to offences of this kind, creates an almost absolute impossibility of getting a conviction, notwithstanding the fact that it is a matter of public notoriety that these establishments exist and that people do frequent them. I confess I have difficulty in seeing that there is any such awful burden thrown on the man, without, as the hon. gentleman says, a chance of his disproving it. It is absolutely open to him to disprove it if he can. The only fact involved is the presumption that that house is a disorderly house-everything else to be proved.

Those are two definite and distinct offences. One person is tried for keeping a disorderly house. Very good. All the evidence necessary for proof of that offence will be produced before the court, and the person's guilt or innocence found as the evidence may show. That is one thing. Now you start with another man for being a frequenter of a disorderly house, a separate and distinct offence. In that case it is incumbent upon the Crown to prove that the house was a disorderly house in the first instance, and that, knowing it to be a disorderly house, this man

frequented it. Those are the two main points in his case. We must not suppose for one moment that the evidence is not ascertainable again. It is much better that there should be some burden of proof thrown upon the Crown and that they should be obliged to produce those witnesses who in the first instance were able to prove that this was a disorderly house. The case may be tried before another judge who has no knowledge of the first trial, yet under this law it would only be necessary for the prosecutor to produce a statement that some time ago-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, at the very moment.

I do not care how long ago; that some time ago this woman was found guilty of keeping a disorderly house. Therefore we start with the premise that the accused frequented this disorderly house with knowledge that it was a house of ill-fame. For centuries it has been the principle that the onus is upon the Crown to prove that a man is guilty. Do not let us get away from that principle.

When a man is brought before the court to answer the charge that he frequented a house of ill-fame the proof is made by five or maybe ten witnesses, in the presence of all the parties interested, and the court then pronounces that it is a house of prostitution. I am satisfied that this amendment is good, for it is not necessary to repeat the proof already given, and it seems to me that justice is done when the same judge in the same court has already received that proof. To recommence that proof would be a loss of time and a waste of money, and absolutely useless.

If the amendment as proposed by the Minister of Justice meets the case explained by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier there is no doubt it is absolutely correct and every hon. member will support it. But unfortunately I do not understand the amendment in that way, and I do not think the amendment to the amendment introduced by the Minister of Justice would meet that case. As it reads now the amendment is open to very serious criticism. As hon. members have already stated, we lay down the principle that an accused person may be presumed to be guilty, although under the general law, such a person is presumed to be innocent until proven guilty. If the minister draws his amendment to meet the case explained by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier
I shall have no objection whatsoever, although as I say, the amendment is open to very serious criticism.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment now reads:
As against any person charged with being or having been at the same time an inmate or frequenter of the same disorderly house.

Being there is one
thing and being tried is another.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
While I do not share the apprehension of hon. gentlemen, and while it does seem to me that the amendment in its present form nine times out of ten would be applied in cases which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier foresees, I have no objection to add the following:
Where the persons so charged are tried or to be tried by -the same court-
I cannot say at the "same time," because one person has to be tried after another, and it may take more than a day to try them all. But if we state there that they are to be tried "by the same court" I think ;we have done sufficient. After all, it is the affair of these inmates and frequenters, whether they chose to stay in court while the keeper of the disorderly house is being tried, and I do not think they are exposed to any very great danger.
The Minister of Justice will see at once that if you say "the same court" it does not necessarily follow that it would be the same judge, because the personnel of the court changes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the circumstances I abandon hope of meeting the requirements of hon. gentlemen. I am satisfied that in amending the clause as I suggest I am going as far as a man can go. From the outset I concede that this involves an exception from the general principle. But our Criminal Code is full of exceptions from that general principle, and why this committee should be so excited with regard to this particular kind of offence and the class of people who get convicted of it, I am at a loss to understand. ,For instance, there exists an exception to the general principle that will make me liable to be convicted of stealing because stolen goods are found in my possession until I make proof to the contrary. I am exposed to that, and nobody gets excited. But that we should attach this importance to seeing that no presumption is created against a person charged with this class of offence, one of the most difficult to establish by direct and positive



proof-well, it seems to me regrettable that this Parliament should be so careful about this particular class of offender. I have tried to go as far as I possibly can to meet the suggestions and requirements. But, if the same court, even if it be not the same judge, has found with regard to the same house on the same day that that house was a disreputable house, I conceive that on the abstract theories and principles that is not res adjudicata against the inmate. If it was, we would not need a provision of the law to cover it. But there are cases where the absolute insistence on abstract principles have worked the most absolute injustice and the greatest failures of justice and have afforded no protection of people deserving of protection. I do feel that the words I have suggested are ample tc cover any possible grievance, but if they do not meet the views of those whose views I am trying to meet, personally I would not think they were necessary at all.

If the accused in a case of this kind says that the crime was not committed; if he has other evidence to adduce or can make further proof, he is not prevented from doing so. It is a simple presumption, and if he wants to go into other proof he has a right to do it.
Now could we not have a vote? We have spent hours on this thing and we have had all possible explanations. Can we have it decided now, and go on?

Is the closure applied? If so, I will have to sit down, but if not, then we have the right to discuss the matter. I do not understand why the Minister of Justice should take these amendments under his wing and hug them to his heart as if they were his own offspring and then get mightily offended if anybody says anything against them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not offended. If the hon. gentleman is under that impression he is greatly mistaken.

I have been a great many years in the House of Commons with the Minister of Justice, sitting opposite him most of the time, and I can tell by this time when he is just a little hot under the collar, if he will permit me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Sometimes you tell it when it is not so.

I notice that this is one of the cases where the right hon. gentleman is quite ready to browbeat us out

of the House, if possible. Now, I have not the slightest sympathy with the subject matter that we are discussing. I would say to any Minister of Justice that if he wants to keep out of trouble, if he wants to avoid wasting time in this way, he will stand behind the grand old principles of the criminal law of England, one of which is that every subject is regarded as innocent until proved guilty, and it is up to the party who lays the charge against him to establish his case. That is an easy position for the Minister of Justice to take, and if he takes it nobody will find fault, but we have been tampering and tinkering and meddling with that principle in this House ever since I came here. We have been getting bolder all the time, and now this grand old principle is disappearing altogether. A man happens to be innocently in a house where he is taking a glass of whisky or a glass of beer, perhaps playing a game of billiards. After he leaves, the people who live there are found to be guilty of keeping a disorderly house, and six months afterwards that conviction may be put up against that man as prima facie evidence of his being a frequenter of that house. He may know nothing about it; he may have forgotten that he ever was there, but it is brought to his memory and that is prima facie evidence of his being guilty of frequenting a house of ill-fame. I say that in accordance with the principles of justice and fair play, in such a circumstance the whole case should have to be proved to the hilt. That is the principle I am fighting for; that is the principle I would always stand for. Why does any minister of Justice wish to tamper or interfere with the liberty of the subject? If we must be forced to swallow these things by a vote, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has suggested, or by closure, all right, but as long as we have the liberty of speech we shall take advantage of every opportunity to submit our views to cool-headed men who will pass judgment upon them as they would upon evidence.
I suggest that the clause be dropped.

I think there should be a limit to the time within which such prosecution should be brought. I rather agree with the hon. member for North Cape Breton that under the provision as it stands a prosecution might be brought any length of time afterwards and one charged with an offence under the section placed in a very unfair position.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am under the impression that there is a time limit for bringing prosecutions in regard to all offences of this nature.

I should think it should be shortened in this case. If the time limit is thirty days for ordinary cases it should be made five in this.
Amendment (Mr. Doherty) agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 29-offender under suspended sentence may be placed on probation:

This is a new provision, and I think something should be said in regard to it. Ic introduces the principle of probation in addition to that of suspended sentence. As the law stands now, the magistrate or judge may give a sus'-pended sentence, but the delinquent goes back to his old surroundings, and the attention of the public should be drawn to the change. Probation has been said by a writer to be "The greatest forward step in a generation in the rational and humane treatment of delinquents." I may point out that the advantages of probation extend not only to keeping the man away from his old associates but to giving him material help. In United States cities where this system has been tried, these are some of the advantages which they get from a probation system:
Finding new living quarters for the family.
Sending children to the country.
Securing homes. .
Arranging for loans.
Teaching mothers how to care for their children.
Securing credit from landlords.
Improving housing and living conditions.
Securing legal advice.
Taking probationers to places of amusement and libraries.
Finding better boarding places; guaranteeing payment of board.
Securing salary increases.
Placing girls in trade schools for special training.
Having board of health improve sanitary condition.
Giving personal instruction to probationers preparing for examinations.
All these advantages have been found to come from adopting this system. Another statement which I might cite from the same author is as follows:
Probation is the outgrowth of a more humane spirit, of a better understanding of what society owes to those who 'go wrong. It is a realization that the debt is not all on one side, an appreciation of the fact that it is better to reclaim a man than it is to make a physical and moral wreck of him.
In New York this result has been found from the system of probation:
As to the results of probation, our records show that 75 per cent of all those placed on probation make good. Many lives that might have been marred have been remade by probation. Many youthful offenders who might have become confirmed criminals have been saved. Many homes have been rescued from destruction. Many women have been lifted from the depths of despair and millions of dollars have been saved to them and their little ones and the community which might have been wasted through prison sentences, loss of jobs and the consequent neglect that flows from incarceration of the family's bread winner.
That is the idea that pervades the principle of probation. By convicting a man or a woman, especially in the younger years, you may place them on the downward career towards crime. By sending them to a kindly but authoritative probation officer, if he brings into operation these ameliorating facts which I have spoken of, these people may be saved for society and society may be saved the expense of treating them continually as criminals. The idea has been studied by a judge who has now become an experienced and capable judge, being the senior judge in York County, Ontario, which has a very large criminal business. He has visited several different cities of the United States with a view of finding out how this can best be brought about and what are the advantages of the courts of probation in that country. Judge Coatsworth has, in a pamphlet presented to the Ontario Government, made a report on that and he comes out strongly in favour of probation. Another book on the Inferior Criminal Courts Act of the city of New York, which I have been sent by promoters of this idea and which is very large and which I will not quote from, shows how the system works there. This movement is supported by these societies of men and women who take up work voluntarily in the large cities especially, work which we ought to do, but which we do not do and which we leave to them. The list which I have here does not contain names of those of a class which I was sorry to hear described by an hon. gentleman here to-day as "hysterical women." These are essentially business men and women and they do an immense amount to help society in all kinds of community work. If the hon. gentleman who used that expression would realize that the use of such a term might deter any woman or man from continuing in this work simply because they are so described in Parliament, he would be the last person to use the term again. For the purpose of showing what a large number of persons are interested in this work and to draw the

attention of the public to the question of probation, I read a few of the fifty or sixty names in order to show that this system has the approval of them all:

I move in
amendment to add as clause 11a of the Bill, the following:
lla. Section three hundred and twenty of the said Act is amended by adding thereto the following words:
"provided he also publishes at the same time-
"(a) any facts, extenuating circumstances or argument which the person likely to be injured by such defamatory matter has set up before such court or at such enquiry; or
"(to) if no such facts, extenuating circumstances or argument have been made known or
made at the time of such publication, then a statement giving such person's explanation or version of the matter."
Section 320 states that newspapers may publish evidence taken in court even though that evidence may be defamatory. Sometimes a complainant files his complaint in court, and the evidence which is given in court is very defamatory to the defendant or the accused. It is published in the newspapers, and some people who read the report form a premature opinion of the case. When, later on, the evidence of the accused is given in court, and is published in the newspapers, it frequently happens that those who have read the complainant's evidence do not read the testimony brought forward by the other side, and they retain the opinion previously formed, which is very damaging to the accused. I know of cases where evidence of the complainant has been published, but the evidence of the defence has not been given to the public. I am aware of a case which occurred about three or four years ago where a man was brought before the court and acquitted, but a certain unscrupulous newspaper, to injure him, published the evidence of the complainant alone. My idea is to provide that the evidence of the complainant shall not be published without the publication, at the same time, of the evidence of the defence; and where the defence is not made at the same time as the complainant's case Is before the court, the newspapers shall not publish the evidence of the complainant without the consent of the other party. This is only fair to those who are brought before the courts, where there is a serious complaint laid against them, and I think it should be made an offence for a newspaper to publish only the evidence of one side, the evidence of the complainant.

What does the hon. member think of newspapers that publish the contents of writs? Certain newspapers make it a habit to hold up people to blackmail by publishing the contents of writs. Some one issues a writ against you charging you with owing money, and so forth, and sends the writ to the newspapers to have it published. I think that something should be done to put a stop to this. For $2.50 I can go and get a writ and charge my hon. friend with owing me $10,000, and have that writ published in the newspapers, and there is no recourse. There should be a stop to that sort of thing; it is a favourite method of blackmail.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: There is much in what the hon. gentleman says, and I have no objection to supporting an amendment to that effect.

There is another kind of injustice. A great wrong is done in the case of election petitions. A petition is filed in which a man is accused of nearly all the crimes in the calendar, and it is published by a hostile newspaper. In nine cases out of ten, the charge is not sustained; it is not brought forward. In the meantime, however, the public is informed that the man is everything but a thief, and I do not know what remedy he has. This is a grave injustice, and many a member of Parliament has suffered therefrom.

I have personal experience of that. When I ran my first election, there were fourteen writs against me, and not one of them was proceeded with. Nevertheless, the contents of those writs were published, the object being to keep the voters from voting for me. Not one of them had the slightest foundation in fact, and they were never brought forward; yet they were published.

They never
hurt a hair of your head.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are dealing with the proceedings of courts, which are essentially public. It is considered, and rightly so, that one of the great guarantees of pure administration of justice is that the proceedings of the courts should all go on in the eyes of the public. Of course, every one cannot be present in court to hear and see.
But everybody would have a right to be there and to hear and to see, and it follows that any man has a right to tell his neighbours when he goes out from the court what it was he heard in court. In the same way the man who has a sheet of paper and a bottle of ink can sit down and write a letter or tell anybody what he saw or heard in the court; and the man who has a printing press and a newspaper has just the same right to tell the people that he can reach. Now, we cannot deprive the people of that right without curtailing the publicity of our court proceedings.
As regards what has been said about election petitions there is no doubt there is a frightful abuse, but the abuse is not in the fact that the newspapers make public the petition-the abuse consists in
tMr. Currie.]
the fact that it is open to people to make reckless charges in an election petition, as it is in fact, and I do not know how it is going to be prevented. At the present time the law requires that there should be an affidavit with the petition, in which the petitioner swears to his sincerity and so forth. Still I believe it is a matter of public knowledge that you can go and buy in a law printer's office a printed form of an election petition which contains, of course, an allegation that a man has violated every section of the statute. That is the election petition. Now it is very difficult to say, if a man may make that election petition and make it a proceeding of the court, that the newspaper would not be entitled to publish it. I am not making that observation without seeing the difficulty of dealing with the subject. Though there may be a real grievance result from it we have got to bear in fnind what I said at the outset, that the publicity of the court proceeding is something that has always been considered to be, perhaps not absolutely essential, but a very valuable feature in connection with our system of the administration of justice.
Now with regard to the particular amendment that is suggested, I would be disposed to think that the present section might well be amended by having ' a proviso to require that the report with which the defamatory matter was concerned should be complete-
Not ex-parte.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Should be complete
and should tell everything.
Both sides should be set forth.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -but that does not entirely meet the case. Because: Take a prolonged trial. The prosecutor makes his case first, and he may take a week. Now it is a serious matter to suggest that you will prevent newspapers day by day publishing what went on in the court. Of course in the prosecutor's case will be set forth everything that can be said against the accused, and that will go to the public day by day unless you intervene to prevent it, and the paper cannot in advance report the defence that is going to be made. Even so, it will be of very little advantage after all for the newspaper to accompany the report of what actually did take place in court with the statement that the defendant said he was going to prove something else later on. It is not easy-

If, at the same time that the evidence for the prosecution is published there is a statement by the accused regarding his case, it would certainly mitigate the damages that the publisher would incur. That is the reason why I have put the second proviso in my amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There may be some truth in that, but if what I started out by saying be true, and I think it is-the court is a public place, and every man has the right to go and hear and see what goes on there, and a right to communicate that to all his neighbours by whatever means of communication he may have at his disposal-if that be true, then it does not seem to me to be quite clear that we have a right to impose upon that man the obligation of inserting something that the accused party chooses to come and say to him. What the ordinary man reads and looks for is a report of what happens in the court. I do not know that he wants interjected into it-here, there and everywhere,-what the defendant says, that he is going to prove this is not true, and after all that is substantially all the defendant can say. I would be prepared if we could do so to frame a proviso that would require that the report made should be a complete report of what transpired.
That would be only an ex-parte report just the same, it would be only the evidence of the complainant.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As long as it is impossible to simultaneously take the evidence of the complainant and the evidence of the defendant, I am afraid the defendant will have to suffer the consequences of the fact that the complainant's evidence is given first. The defendant will get his innings when he comes to give his evidence and he will publish it. But it does not really seem to me to be practicable to require that every time a newspaper publishes the day's proceedings in court it must be compelled to publish another statement in which the defendant says that when it comes to his turn he is going to prove all sorts of things. After all, has not the public got some sort of judgment? Does it not know this is the plaintiff's case and that the defendant is going to get his chance? I know that people do not always read all the report, and unfortunately the public is very apt to believe sensational accusations and never look at the defence. I would suggest that we allow the Bill to 'be passed
as it stands. I will consult with the hon. gentleman in the meantime and if we can possibly agree upon the amendment before the Bill goes to its third reading I will allow the measure to be sent back to committee and put the amendment in.

The
point raised by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is more important than this amendment. I think you would easily stop people from issuing the pleadings which the hon. member refers to and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) also. Those things can be stopped, but I do not see how you can stop the publishing of evidence where the case is actually under trial.

Mr. Chairman, during recess I had a conversation with the Minister of Justice and the deputy minister, who both agreed and admitted that the amendment embodied a very good reform, but ata the same time there was some objection to the amendment and they asked me to withdraw it, which I will do. But I should like to remind hon. members that as the law now stands advantage may be taken of it to the detriment of an absolutely innocent person. As I pointed out before six o'clock, an hon. member of this House was charged with a very serious offence about two months ago. The charge was laid by political opponents evidently to injure his reputation. He was brought before the courts in Montreal, and the evidence of the complainant, which was of a damaging nature, was reported by the Canadian press in every paper in Canada. The malice behind the charge was so apparent that the judge who presided at the trial dismissed it without even hearing the defence, and the hon. member was honourably acquitted. The news of the acquittal in the form of a few lines was published in only a few newspapers, and some of the journals which had published the complainant's evidence at length did not even insert the announcement that the hon. member had been acquitted. In fact La Minerve, a paper subsidized, I believe, by this Government, although it published the evidence of the complainant conspicuously, hardly mentioned the acquittal. As the law stands there is no redress, and the press can

publish damaging evidence without also publishing any announcement of the accused being honourably acquitted or stating what his defence is.
This was the reason for my moving the amendment. I hope the Minister of Justice will remember his promise and so amend the law that in future newspapers will be prevented from giving publicity to such damaging evidence against innocent parties. On this understanding 1 beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
Amendment withdrawn.

Kennel keeping is an important industry in which a large amount of money is invested. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say that the modified fees were made upon suggestions that came to us and that we accepted.

I have known witnesses to spend from three days to, perhaps, two weeks attending trials, and the minister knows that a dollar will not much more than pay for a meal in many places and not that much in many others.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The former tariff
allowed witnesses 75 cents for each day attending trial. The present tariff allows one dollar.

It is not necessary to point out that that is utterly inadequate. I do not presume it is the intention to pay the full cost to each witness, but the amount is so far short of the actual cost that some change should be made.

On the other hand we have 'to consider a little the litigants who have to pay these costs. What change would the hon. gentleman suggest? If we made the fee $1.50, that would be double
the previous fee and witnesses have got along all these years with 75 cents.

I have heard many complaints on that score. The actual expense witnesses in the country would be put to would be anything from $3 to $5; in the cities, the expense would be greater than that. Two dollars would be the very minimum for each day attending trial.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To meet the hon.
gentleman's suggestion, which probably has some weight behind it, if we may return, as I presume we have returned, to section 24, I would move to amend section 24 by inserting in lieu of "one dollar," the words "two dollars," so as to provide that the fee of the witness shall be $2 per day while attending trial.

I notice that the fees were enlarged both as to travelling and attendance. Formerly, a witness got only ten cents a mile for travelling; now he gets 15 cents, and instead of 75 cents a day he get $1 a day. I rather think the amounts should be left as they are. There is an increase of 25 cents on the day's attendance and 5 cents a mile on travelling. If a man comes any considerable distance, he gets 15 cents a mile. As the minister mentioned, the fees were always made small so as to make it possible for the poor man to go into court and get justice. If the fees are made large, he will not be able to pay them, and he will have to waive his rights in court. I would be disposed to leave the fees as they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not any very
strong feeling on the subject; but my attention being called to the matter by the hon. member, (Mr. Campbell) it seems to me that as regards the average man who is called as a witness, his day is worth more than $1.50 to him. I do not think we will do any real injustice if we leave it at $1 or make it $1.50. If the hon. gentleman will consider this matter from the witness' point of view, it is certainly pretty hard for a man who is earning $5 a day to have to sacrifice his day for a dollar in order to be of service to his neighbour, or, if you will, to the administration of justice. In our civil courts, witnesses' taxation fees, when I last knew of them, certainly exceeded one dollar a day. They were a dollar a day when I first began to practise law many years ago, and I must confess that I was surprised to find that they were so small still. On the other hand, we must

consider the tax that is put upon the unfortunate litigant who has to pay these fees.

It may happen that the time of a witness who has no interest in the case will be more important than that of the litigant. Why should he be compelled to pay $2.50 to $3 a day to help out one of the litigants?

I am sure the Minister of Justice would like to have uniformity in the law as much as possible. I am not familiar with the fees in the other provinces; but in the province from which I come, in a civil suit, the witness gets one dollar a day and ten cents a mile for travel. By this proposed legislation we are going to create the anomaly that if two witnesses are travelling ten miles, one going to a criminal court and the other to a civil court, the one going to a civil court gets $1 a day and ten cents a mile for travel and the other going to a criminal court gets $1.50 a day and fifteen cents a mile for travel. There is bound to be trouble. I would like to have uniformity, at least as far as our province is concerned. If it is left as it is in this schedule, there will be no great trouble, but if the change is made^ the man who goes to the criminal court will be 50 cents per day, and 5 cents per mile, to the good.

I would like the minister to give the committee some further information on his clause. When the resolution was under discussion a few days ago I took the liberty of raising some objections to the provisions of this clause, and I was under the impression that the minister would have some further explanation to make at this stage. speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not in a position to withdraw the clause. We still think it is proper that the marking should be done. I do not know that I can go further than I went before as regards the grounds on which we think it ought to be done, but I certainly undertake that in the regulations that are drawn up we shall try to be reasonable, and my hon friend need have no fears that the marking will have injurious results.

It is only fair to this
committee that we should have same idea as to the provisions that will be enacted in regard to this feature of the tariff. I had hoped that the committee would be given a specific list of the merchandise that would be branded by the Customs Department. The range of merchandise that comes through the Customs Department is a very wide one, and the number of items which it will be possible to brand without injury is very limited. It ought to be practicable for the minister or his officials to frame some specific list for the information of importers; otherwise importers will, as heretofore, place their contracts abroad, and will have nothing to guide them along these lines. I appeal to the minister to submit for the consideration of the committee, a specific list of items which they intend to' have branded. The question should not

be left to the discretion of the officials of the department, because they have not the technical knowledge of merchandise that would enable them to come to a proper decision as to the items that can be marked without injury. Furthermore, if the question is left open, there may be two opinions as to the possibility or the desirability of branding certain merchandise. A merchant might place a contract with a British manufacturer and decide that it was neither possible nor desirable to brand the goods, and when they arrived at the Customs Department, the officials might have an entirely different opinion about the matter. Consequently under this resolution, the first step that would be taken would be to penalize the merchant to the extent of 10 per cent additional tariff on the goods imported. Then the shipment would be held up until the point had been threshed out by the Customs Department. I see room for grave difficulty in connection with this provision. As a matter of fact, there is no real advantage to be gained by this proposal. The assigned reason is that it will make it clear to purchasers just what class of goods they are getting, and where they have been manufactured. Well, I submit that the real consideration, after all, in any purchase, is value and service, and 99 per cent of purchasers care not one whit where the goods they buy are made; all they desire to know is that the goods are of a certain quality and are good value for the money they pay. If the goods are reliable, and meet with their approval, that is all that should be expected. To go beyond that and enact this proposed legislation will only create hardship and friction, and, in my opinion, the minister will experience a great deal more trouble in connection with this provision that he was beset with during the past year in the enforcement of the luxury tax. That tax was only a small matter compared to the possible results of this provision, from the point of view of the trouble which the minister and his officials will be faced with.
