Does that Act not
enumerate the articles that must be branded? How will the purchaser of merchandise ever know what is required of him by the Customs Department under this resolution? You are really enacting a law with which it is impossible to comply.

I think there is much force in the contention of my hon. friend from Renfrew. I have received a letter from a firm in Quebec city which imports a certain class of goods, and from that letter I desire to quote the following extract:
We understand that this ruling does not mean that the containers or packages of the items are to be stamped, but each individual item. We have been wondering if this ruling is going to be rigidly enforced with respect to Calendars, Pictures, Calendar Pads, Blotters. Pans, and such other items that we sell you from time to time, for it will mean that such articles, where it is possible, will have to be run through the press "for an extra printing, thereby, of course, adding considerable to the cost of the goods, and in some cases it will be practically impossible to apply the ruling, for instance on Calendar Pads. The putting of such an imprint on Calendar Pads and Pad Covers and other small items would not only be impracticable, but In some cases it would really add an additional cost which would be more than the actual cost of the goods themselves.
I wish to draw to the attention of the minister what is stated in this letter, and I shall be glad if he will give some explanation that will allay the fear of these gentlemen.

Perhaps the minister will allow us to have a little say on this subject in committee; I make that suggestion in perfect good faith. Possibly the minister in one speech could answer ten interpolations from this side or the other. I am not satisfied personally with the answer which my hon. friend has made to the speech of the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow). All the answer that was vouchsafed my hon. friend

was that this is being done in other countries, and the country particularly mentioned is the United States. Well, that is no justification whatsoever for the expedient toeing adopted toy the Parliament of Canada. We are governing Canada, and the fact that something is done in the United States, or Britain, or Timbuctoo, is no satisfactory reason as to why it should be done here. I should like the minister to tell us, if he borrowed the expedient from the United States, where he borrowed the reasons for its being proposed to toe put into operation here. What is the object of this marking? What is the reason for it? Will additional expense be incurred by some one by the marking, and if so, toy whom? Who will discharge the expense? All additional trouble in this world means additional expense.
If there be trouble and expense in connection with trading, it makes the article traded in more expensive, more costly, and it is to that extent an embarrassment to trading when we want it to toe freer, when we want to do something to stop the rot that is taking place in the trade of Canada. When my hon. friend is answering I should like him to tell us what effect he thinks this marking will have upon the trade of the country. What is the object or the reason for it? Will it incur expense; will it mean employing more government officials; what will be its effect upon trade? Is it not clearly a continuation of bureaucratic practices somewhere which we had to have recourse to of necessity during the war, perhaps, tout which we would be better without now. I had occasion to tell the Government and the House the other day that we do not need a Government to help trade, we do not need a Government to interfere with trade. If people are left alone they will trade, it is natural to them to do so. Now I have put my questions specifically to the minister, and I hope in answering them he will let the United States alone and reply to these specific questions.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was just
waiting for a moment to see if there were any other questions so that I might be able to adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend from Red Deer. Perhaps there are other hon. gentlemen who desire to ask questions.

Is there not also an ambiguity about the proviso which reads:
That all goods imported into Canada after the date of the coming into force of this section which do not comply with the foregoing requirements-

and so on. Well, there are two requirements, and one is that goods capable of toeing stamped sfhall toe stamped. But goods which are not capable of being stamped are classed under this proviso. Therefore I think the wording of the proviso should toe made clearer than it now is. Otherwise it would, in my opinion, preclude all goods whether they were stamped or whether they were not stamped, whether they were capable of being stamped Or incapable of being stamped.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better answer the last question first. I submit to my hon. friend that the clause is very clear:
That all goods imported into Canada which are capable of being marked, stamped, branded or labelled without injury, shall be marked.
I think that is fairly clear, tout if there is any doubt about it let us .make it absolutely clear. My idea is that if we add any more language to the section we may somewhat becloud what would appear to me to be a pretty clear sentence.
Then my hon. friend from Quebec (Mr. Lapointe) points out the difficulties in regard to the marking of printed matter. Well, the answer to him pretty nearly answers my hon. friend from Red Deer. I should say, in the first instance, that there is no difficulty whatever about branding books, calendars, and so forth, showing where they are made. The name of the printer is usually shown, and I do not know that the additional words are going to be a very great burden. I would not think so. If marking and printing can toe done easily I think it can be done easily toy people in the printing business. I might further point out-and this is a question which I know the hon. gentleman from Red Deer will be much interested in-that the printers, and the printers' unions, who were particularly desirous of having this done, illustrated the fact that they were subject to the competition of printers in other countries who were getting approximately I am not sure of the exact figures-one-tenth of their wages. They said "If we are to be subject to that competition let the Canadian people at least know where they are buying these articles from." Cigar bands, and the like, in connection with which there is a good deal of printing in Canada are subject to competition of that class from abroad; and I will tell my hon. friend from Red Deer that I certainly desire to protect Canadian printers against a standard of living at least ten degrees

below that of the Canadian labour man. That is one of the reasons for this provision.
My hon. friend does not mean competition from the United States, I am sure.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was certainly not referring to labour in the United States; I was not referring at all to the United States. As a matter of fact, the points in connection with which this claim was-rightly or wrongly and I believe lightly-made by Canadian labour were Japan on the one side and the Continent on the other. There is no complaint about the United States in connection with printing. That was one reason why we thought marking should be done. I will tell my hon. friend another reason why we thought it necessary. We thought it would be a good thing to make it just a little more difficult to impose a fraud on the public than it now is-just a little bit. I have an idea, for example, that the public, when they think they are buying an English knife, should get an English knife. I do not know whether that will appeal to my hon. friend from Red Deer or not, but it did appeal to me.
Mr, CLARK: No.	#

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not appeal to my hon. friend?
No, because I would like to take care of myself in buying a knife; I do not want my hon. friend to help me at all in making such a purchase.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not
intend to legislate for one minute for people who have the knowledge of cutlery that my hon. friend has. I am thinking of the Canadian public who, perhaps, do not know just exactly the different brands of steel and the different kinds of manufacture quite as well as my hon. friend may. Now those were the two main reasons why this was done and why we are standing on it. I am very glad that my hon. friend points out that we should not consider what is being done in other countries including the United States. Simply because a thing is done in England does not mean that it is a good thing to be done here. I entirely agree with my hon. friend that our fiscal policy must be dictated by the needs and interests of the Canadian nation, rather than by what England finds it pays her to do. The only reason why I referred to the United
States was to illustrate the practical working out of the measure. Over there they do not bring down a Bill with a long list of names, saying exactly what is to be done with every one of the articles named. They simply bring in a declaration that articles which can be marked without injury, shall be marked so as to show the ' country of origin.

I
understand the minister to say that when the article is already marked it will not be necessary to mark it again. That is, if there are words on the book or the article that is imported from the United States, or some other foreign country, into Canada, which indicate where it came from, it will not be necessary to mark it specially. For example, the Government distribute penholders to members, and I happen to have one on my desk which I got from the distribution office. I find that it is marked "Eagle Pencil Company, New York".
New York?

New
York. I presume an article of that description which already bears an indication of where it was made will not have to be marked again. I can understand, however, where there will toe great difficulty, and I sympathize with the view taken by my hon. friend from South Renfrew. If the minister is to issue a special list for the use of importers so that they will know what goods are to be marked, he will have to be very careful in its compilation. For some time I (have no doubt great trouble will arise through this regulation. The clause seems to require that the goods themselves ibe marked, not the wrapper or container. But supposing you get a bundle of white silk ribbon, to mark it in many places would damage it and render it practically useless.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You could not mark that at all.

That may be one of the class of articles that would be exempt. At the same time the importer might not know that, and if it was left to the discretion of the customs officer the latter might raise difficulties with the importer. The penalty is very severe-unnecessarily so for a regulation of this kind which is entirely new in this country. It strikes me that levying a penalty of $1,000 for omitting to place

this mark on goods that may not he worth ten cents is ridiculous. There is no reason why we should frighten people with penalties of this kind, for it is no crime to import goods, and I cannot understand why the minister should want to levy such a heavy fine on a trader who omitted to comply with this regulation.
I also favour the proposal made toy my hon. friend from South Renfrew that in place of advertising the country where the goods are made, as for example on this penholder, it would toe better to say that it was made in Canada. If we are going to put a stamp on imported goods there is no necessity why we should advertise and build up the trade of foreign countries. Such a regulation as this would toe a very fine advertisement for the United States. For example, if I touy a (pair of boots from a merchant in Canada and they fit me, and I want another pair of the same make, if I find on the soles of those boots that they were made in New York or Boston that is the best sort of advertisement the American manufacturer can have. They have realized that in England, where they started this idea some time ago I understand, and they changed their regulations, which now, instead of requiring the country of origin to be marked, directs that all imported goods shall be marked " not made In England." That seems to be a very reasonable regulation. I have not heard the minister say that he would accept it, but for the life of me I cannot understand why we should go to the trouble and expense of advertising foreign countries and helping them to sell their goods.

The section reads:
That all goods imported into Canada which are capable of being marked, stamped, branded or labelled, without injury, shall be marked, stamped, branded or labelled, etc.
So this would not apply to silk ribbons or to any other goods that might be injured toy stamping or marking. The section does not provide that goods have to toe branded to indicate the place of manufacture, tout merely to indicate the country of origin. So if goods are made ift Germany they must be branded " made in Germany," and likewise goods made in England or any other ountry would be similarly branded to indicate the country of origin. There is no reason why goods should toe branded to indicate the particular town or city from which they come; but I may tell my hon. friend from
[Mr. Sinclair. 1
Guysborough that very few manufacturers who are not ashamed of their goods do not now mark them not only to indicate the town or city where they are made but the company who manufacture them.
They do it for the advertisement.

Absolutely; and it is no hardship on anybody who imports goods to mark on them the country of origin. We need not wonder about the cost. No one can calculate the cost of marking these goods, because the men who-take a pride in their products will mark them, unless they are trying to evade and deceive, and that is what we want to avoid and what we should avoid.
I discussed this proposition at considerable length when the resolution was before the committee, but it seems to me I will be compelled to cover pretty much the same territory again-
No, no; please.

-to emphasize the point I endeavoured to emphasize on that occasion. The member for North Oxford seems to think that if imported goods are branded the consumer will be assured of getting the proper quality of merchandise.

He would soon know
from the brand.

That, in the opinion of the Minister of Finance, is only one of the features. When the resolution was before us a few days ago he laid particular stress on the fact that it would enable the consumer to understand and to know just exactly where the merchandise was manufactured. There is a good deal in what the hon. member for Guysborough said in that connection, and much more than appears on the surface. If this Bill passes in its present form, it will mean that the trade of Canada will be forced to advertise on their counters the merchandise of foreign countries. That is one of the weakest parts of this section. It will compel our importers to distribute advertising matter for Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Czecho-Slovakia, Italy, the British Isles, and other countries. I insist that if the minister must have a provision of this kind he should follow the British system and have all imported goods branded, " Not manufactured in Canada". That is the system in force in the British Isles, all their imported goods are branded

" Not manufactured in the British Isles," and I do not think we can make any mistake in following their example. The merchants and manufacturers there took exception to a provision similar to this, and the law was changed accordingly. This is a very unwise proposition to force on the business of this country. In the first place it requires that all goods which are capable of being marked must be marked in a conspicuous place. It still leaves the question of what is a conspicuous place open for debate between the importer, the maun-facturer and the customs officials. Supposing the importer does his level best to comply with the requirements of this Bill, and his shipment of goods arrive in the customs office, each article duly marked in his judgment in compliance with the Act, and the customs officer says. " These are not branded in a conspicuous place. I will hold up this entire shipment and will penalize you to the extent of 10 per cent to start with." Then, the next thing is that the goods will not be allowed to leave the Customs office until they have been branded under the supervision of the customs officials. This may mean a delay of weeks and months in the case of perishable merchandise, and after they are released, even though they have not been injured by branding or stamping, they may be out of date and considerably depreciated in value. I do wish -the minister and his deputy would give real consideration to this view; it is a view that they cannot escape. Take the law that was passed last year in regard to manufacturers collecting the luxury tax. All hon. members know the difficulties that arose in that regard. The minister assured the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) and the member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) that harness makers, blacksmiths and tailors would not be classified as manufacturers; yet we know what happened. These trades were put to enormous trouble during the year; they were made to pay a license fee and compelled to collect sales tax as manufacturers, although they were not manufacturers and although the minister assured us on the floor of the House that they would not be so considered. An expensive lawsuit has resulted; it was decided against the Government only last week, and the Minister of Finance assures me that the Government have had to pay the costs. Now, here is cause for any number of lawsuits and any amount of trouble.
Why, you cannot get two men in the same line of business who -have the same ideas as to the branding of merchandise. How,
then, can you expect a proper decision when the conflict of opinion is between a government official and an importer? You cannot find in Webster's dictionary any words adequate to describe the character of this provision. It provides that the goods must be marked in a conspicuous place. Well now, that is pretty plain language, and I know from experience the interpretation that the customs officials will give to it. Take the line of the merchandise I mentioned the other day, silk stockings, which we import in large quantities. The only conspicuous place on a silk stocking is the leg; the toe would not be considered by the minister's officials as a conspicuous place. He says that the marking on the toe will be accepted by him, but we know from our experience of last year that the inland revenue officers will have a different opinion in the matter. Moreover, the customs officers themselves will have different opinions in different parts of the country and there will be no end of trouble, no end of turmoil from one end of Canada to the other. It is impossible, I say, to make this Act workable. Then, it is provided that the goods must be marked in detail; every item in the package must be marked. I appeal to the hon. gentleman's common sense; I do submit that this provision will cause an immense amount of trouble and will involve expense which will add to the cost of the merchandise and increase the price to the consumer.
I have already called attention to the penalty clause providing that 10 per cent shall be added to the cost of the merchandise if in the judgment of the customs officer it fails to comply with the requirements of this Act. Mr. Chairman, this Act has not been properly thought out. I do not like to use the word, because I have the highest admiration for the minister, but it seems to me to be a half-baked measure; it has not run the gauntlet of careful criticism and consideration. An Act of this kind, if it is to be enforced, should be worked out by men who are experienced in this line of work and who know what they are talking about; men who can say what lines of merchandise can be branded and what lines cannot be branded without destroying or depreciating their value. The penalty clause read by the minister the other night as being in operation in United States is slightly different from that 'which is adopted here. In fact, the omission of one word makes a big difference. If the provisions contained in the third section of this paragraph are insisted on, it leaves

the matter in such a position that no one importing merchandise can escape the penalty, and it is a very severe one-a thousand dollars or a year's imprisonment or both. The penalty applies to any person who violates any of the provisions relating to the marking, stamping, branding or labelling of any imported goods. That is, if a man fails to have the merchandise marked, or if he fails to have it marked in the place where the customs officer thinks it should be marked; if he fails to do a thousand and one little things which he is liable innocently to omit to do-because he has nothing to guide him' in this Act; there are no definite instructions-then he is liable to this heavy penalty. In the United States Act which was read by the minister a few nights ago the word "fraudulently" was used after the word "shall" in the third line. I think that is only a reasonable provision. If a man innocently violates the Act, he is liable to penalty, though he may not have had the least intent of breaking the law. I really think the House will have gone insane if it endorses this provision. This part of the Act should be deleted entirely, or further consideration given to it before it becomes law.

I do not propose to delay the committee to any considerable extent in the few observations which I wish to make concerning this Bill. But I do not wish this part of the Bill to pass without registering ,a most emphatic protest. I want to remind the Minister of Finance that last year he passed a luxury tax provision, and he did so in spite of the expert advice given him by the member for South Renfrew. He proceeded along the line of error and finally had to admit the error by taking off the luxury tax in the middle of the Christmas season. Now, I have some respect for the out-and-out protectionist, although he is making a mistake-the man who comes out in manly fashion and says: "I am going to raise the tariff; I think it is a good thing for the country." I can respect his sincerity and his courage, although I may have a very unfavourable opinion of his economic knowledge and judgment. But this sort of protection, this sort of pin-prick protection-not only am I opposed to it economically, but I have little respect for that sort of proceeding. I wish I could shake this Government out of its smug self-satisfaction, because I think that if I did I would be conferring a benefit on the country. The Minister of Marine is spending
[ Mr, PeiHow.l
millions of dollars of the people's money for what? With the ostensible purpose of increasing Canada's trade. This is just a comparison I am making-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member in discussing this clause, is certainly not in order in making a comparison between the conduct of the minister in charge of the present legislation and that of the other ministers of the Government.

Well, without making any comparison at all between these gentlemen, I submit to the committee with all confidence that what the Minister of Finance is doing, no doubt unwittingly and perhaps with the best intentions in the world, is tripping up commerce, pushing pins into commerce, interfering with commerce. You will never make Canada prosperous by interfering in this underhand and small way with the trade of the country. It will cost money to do what is here provided, and that cost will have to be met by some one. The only way by which we shall return to economic prosperity in this country is by freeing trade, not by putting shackles upon it and not by tieing it up with small threads in this way. The minister has read Gulliver's Travels. He will remember that when Gulliver came to Lilliput, he was asleep and the Lilliputians tied his brawny arms and strong legs up with little threads, and finally he was unable to move. That is what the minister is doing with commerce- tieing it up with small, mistaken interferences with the right of people to carry on their business in their own way.

I have listened with very great patience to my hon. friend's reply to a very small portion of the questions that I put to him, and I have heard another very explicit charge against this proposed legislation from the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow). I want to tell the minister-and I hope he will keep quite cool while I try to get my difficulties in this matter solved by him- that so far I am much more impressed with the objections of the hon. member for South Renfrew than I am by the explanations of the minister. I asked the minister very politely, if somewhat emphatically, the reason for this legislation, and the only reason that he gave was that ihe would like to protect the Canadian public in buying their knives. I am very grateful to him that he excluded me from his tender care. I want to assure him that a large number of the Cana-

dian public would be willing to free him from further trouble in their case. The minister and I have diametrically opposite views as regards how people trade. When I go to buy a calf from a neighbour, the matter is one between my neighbour and me, and I do not want the minister to come and help me to buy my calf and my neighbour does not want him to help ihim to sell it.	In the wider
field of international trade a condition of mutual trust is to be found on a larger scale as between the importer and the exporter, then between the importer and the retailer, and finally between the retailer and the customer. Human beings have been so constituted that whether they be exporters, importers, retailers or customers, on the whole they are better doing their own business in the world than being helped by petty little details arranged by the Department of Finance and consented to by the minister pro tern. That is my view of trade on general principles.
I hope I have been explicit and clear enough, and that the minister will understand me.
I addressed a number of other questions which my hon. friend failed to pay any attention to ; in fact, he seemed to be very anxious to get back at me and make it a debating point. That is the easiest thing in the world to do; but that is not worth while if we want to facilitate the business of the House and to get away from here some little time before Christmas. This is not a matter of debate between the minister and myself; it is a matter of his clearing away our doubts about the propriety of this legislation. The hon. member for South Renfrew is, I understand, a merchant; he understands about trade; he is not a lawyer, and I believe he could give the minister points in the matter of trade and then not lose. My hon. friend stakes his commercial reputation on the statement that this is going to give rise to an infinity of trouble in trade. Is that the minister's obiect? Does he believe the hon. member? Le( me ask the minister to give me some guidance in this matter. Who is going to make the examination for the marks on the various articles imported? Where is that going to be done? Perhaps the minister can answer that without leaving his seat.
In the customs house.

Then every parcel has to be opened and every article examined. The Minister of Customs has
an assistant now, but I would rather not deal with the assistant; I want to deal with headquarters. Supposing, however, the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is well informed, I think, in his assertion, there is prima facie evidence that the hon. member for South Renfrew understands the matter. He says that there will be a great deal of trouble. I put this to the minister, that if the articles in question are only a gross of pairs of stockings-and that would not be a large import-and every stocking has to be marked on every toe, who is going to look at the toes of the stockings for the marks?
The mark has to be in a conspicuous place.

I understood the other day that my hon. friend got from the minister the concession that it had not to be in a conspicuous place; that it was to be on the toe. I would like to know if he has found out from prospective wearers if they want the toes of their stockings marked at all. I should like to know if he has endeavoured to find out what effect this is going to have on business. ,1 am going into details to show my hon. friend calmly and reasonably what the situation will be, and I hope he will imitate my tone and temper. I hope he will explain to me who is going to do this marking. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) gets up and utters three sentences of an explanation and then wanders out into the lobby thinking he has settled the whole matter. As a matter of fact, he has not settled anything, but has merely given an opinion.
To return to the question which my hon. friend did not answer, this is all trouble- trouble to the markers in the country from which the goods come, and believe me, English traders want to be paid for their trouble, and their customers will pay them. The importer brings the material in, but he sells it to the retailer. The profit is secure to all the dealers, and the whole thing comes upon the poor consumer at the finish. That is the Government's panacea and has been from the start for improving the trade conditions of Canada. If there is any financial trouble, the recipe of the Government has been: "Give the consumer another clout on the head." That is the recipe of the Government for improving our trade conditions. That is the way in which this will operate. Even if the minister will not protect me in the buying of a knife, if he excludes me from

the benefits of his tender care bestowed upon the general public there will be trouble on the American side and1 on the British side wherever he enacts that these marks shall be made, and the Canadian people will pay for it. If I am wrong in this, the minister has left me wrong, because he did not answer my question when I first asked it. I have, therefore, had to explain to him in more detail what my difficulties are and have had to ask the question twice: Will this be an additional expense, and who will pay it? As regards this marking, is it not going to be a real obstacle in the way of trade? I do not care to use the language of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster)-not that there was anything particularly harmful but I want to be careful not to irritate my hon. friend's feelings at this period of the session. I do not want to talk about pin-pricks. I am not trying to pin-prick anybody; I am trying to see whether this is going to increase the trade of Canada and the comfort of the Canadian people or to decrease both, and for the life of me I cannot see but that it will be baneful in its effects. I cannot see the benefit of this legislation; I do not believe the minister is called upon to protect the' whole of the Canadian people in buying all of these articles. I have, however, asked him the question: Will it increase the expense of the trading operation, because nobody contends that the stocking will be better for wearing on account of the mark? The whole tendency would be for it to be worse at that particular point, because there would be the wear caused by putting on the mark, and so with the various other articles. Will not this examination, which my hon. friend from North Simcoe says will be carried out, not lead to the increase of Government officials? Is the whole thing not an unnecessary interference of Government with an operation that would be on the whole better left in the hands of the people themselves, who, after all, when they grow up do not want to be treated as children. If ever I met a people in the world who insist upon their whole manhood and womanhood after they have grown from their 'teens, it is the Canadian people.
I hope I have made my points clear and not taken too much time about it, and I hope that when the minister answers this time he will cover the whole ground, so that I shall not need to say anything more.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will try and
do so. I do not know that I will try to emulate my hon. friend, because if I did

so I am afraid I should have to engage in a little bit of scolding that would be entirely beyond my powers. I have taken notes as accurately as I could of my hon. friend's questions, and the first question to be answered is:	Will this increase the
expense of the operation? There is no doubt about one thing and that is that sometimes the very cheapest of all commodities, cheap sacks, and cheap bags, for instance, are all marked with the name of the maker, often the trade-mark, usually the address, and very often the country. If my hon. friend wants to find something that is cheaper than anything else, let him look at a cheap jack-knife. Even that is marked. If my hon. friend goes down the street to-day and buys a pair of socks-I refer to socks because my hon. friend specializes on stockings-he will find that the cheapest sock he can buy carries its trade-mark.
Does my hon. friend propose a mark in addition to that?
Keep quiet; let the minister answer.

My hon.
friend must keep quiet. This is between the minister and me. I would like the hon. member for Simcoe not to waste the time of this committee. The minister and I are trying to get through, and I would like to call your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that the hon. member for Simcoe, without rising in his place, is behaving in a most disorderly manner, interrupting his own minister, and obstructing the business of the House.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I was
saying, on the cheapest sock you can buy, you will find the name clearly stamped. Now I do not think it would cost very much more, the name and trade-mark being already there, to add the name of the country.
Am I to understand that the minister proposes a mark in addition to that which the maker puts on?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I certainly
propose one thing, and one thing only, and that is that the name of the country of origin shall be shown. I am not interested in trade-marks; I am not interested in names and addresses; I am interested in one thing only and that is that the Canadian public shall know from whom they are buying. It is, of course, a usual thing to have more or less trouble

when a change is made, but I may tell my hon. friend that so far I have received only one letter objecting to what is being done. I may tell him another thing. Either he or the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) stated that we were compelling the advertising of foreign goods in Canada by this marking. Now, so far, the manufacturers, for whom my hon. friend professes fears, have not made the slightest objection to this legislation-not one of them. On the other hand, the importers are making some objection. Now I would like to ask this question: If it be a bad thing for Canadian manufacturers and Canadian production that we should insist on the country of origin being shown-that we should insist, if you like, on the goods of a foreign country being advertised in Canada-why is it that the only people who are complaining of this legislation are the importers whose interest it is to advertise the foreign as against the homemade article?
Because the importers have the trouble. That would be my answer.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon.
friend has not appreciated my point, but the fault is entirely mine. I was just endeavouring to point out an inconsistency which appears to me to be perfectly apparent. It is alleged that the effect' of this legislation will be to advance the sales of imported goods, because of the forced advertisement which they will get. If that is bad for Canadian production, how is it we have received not one complaint of this legislation so far from the manufacturers in Canada.
Another question was:	where is the
marking to be done? Where is the list going to be drawn up? How is it going to be put in force? The list of goods will be drawn up in Ottawa, it will be printed and circulated; it will be placed in the hands of every single customs official at points of entry.
The marking ought to be done, and will be done, in the country of origin. It is now being done in the country of origin in the case of a great many goods of the better class. It is now being done in the country of origin in so far as importations to countries having similar legislation to this are concerned.
Where is the inspection to take place? The inspection will take place where the goods are examined. All goods coming in
have to be examined by the customs officers now. In connection with the larger question of valuing, and inspecting goods passed for customs, a small amount of extra work will be imposed upon the officials to see whether the article is properly marked. This will be done at the customs ports through which the goods pass. The work will be done by exactly the same man that is already doing it; there will be no increase in the number of customs officials. I think I have answered the list of questions in regard to which my hon. friends desires information. If there are any more questions I shall try to answer them.

I was very much interested in the speech of the Minister of Finance in connection with this new duty which he is proposing on goods coming into the country. I thought that we could all safely heave a sigh of relief that the minister was about though with his new taxation proposals, but here he comes with another Bill. Is there any telling when the end will be.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the same matter that has been before the House already.

It is possibly the
same matter, I suppose, on the same principle as the man who was going all over the continent and finding at every hotel at which he stopped a herring cooked in a different ,way. Every time he saw it, he said "You are the same red herring". Well, this may be the same red herring, although it is cooked in a different form. We had some criminal legislation going through this afternoon which reminded me of the story of a little girl who had a favourite pet dog. She heard they were going to cut its tail off and pleaded very hard with the executioner that if it was absolutely necessary to cut off the tail of her dear little dog, she hoped it would be done one piece at a time. She thought that it would be less painful that way. Evidently the Minister of Finance thinks that instead of giving us his objectionable legislation all at once he will save us some inconvenience by giving it to us a little at a time; but I think it would be better to have one fell stroke at once and have done with the whole thing, instead of introducing Acts of this kind from day to day. Now, this proposal says that every article that can be marked must be marked. In this connection, it has occurred to me that my old

Scotch friend would have same difficulty in complying with the law. I refer to the shrewd man who, on one occasion, complained of the dishonesty of the English, as he had a right to do, when he imported one hundred thousand dozens of needles and said: "After I had counted them, I found I was ten short". I wonder what would become of him if he had to examine closely each one of the needles to see that it was stamped. It is not impossible to have a needle stamped, and I would ask my hon. friend if he really would insist on his officials counting every needle that comes into the country to see that it is duly stamped, and, if it is not istamped, whether it is his intention to exact the penalty? I am sure the minister, who is a humane man, is not disposed to be unscrupulous, except in so far as he gives in to his officials, and would see to it that people were not penalized to an enormous extent in connection with goods of this kind. The speech of the member for Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow), stands unanswered. Why should we give people this extra trouble? Who is complaining about a web of cloth as to whether it comes from the Old Country or any place else, so long as he gets his suit properly made to his satisfaction? If a lady goes into a store in Ottawa to buy a pair of boots and they suit her, she is not going to make a row because there is no stamp on them. If the leather is all right, and the boots are of the right style and meet her approval in every way, she is not going to look around to ascertain whether it has any particular stamp on it or not. The truth is that this is another form of protection. I get a great deal of advertisement and1 praise for being a protectionist. I do not try to escape from that reputation at all in many things that are proper and right, but I think that this is a kind of protection which will make it difficult to get goods into the country. It will profit nobody, but, on the other hand, will greatly inconvenience the officials of the department, the manufacturers, and those who do business. It will not serve any good purpose; if it could I certainly should not be opposed to it, because I want to help those who seem to have put some thought and time into this matter. Your predecessor in the Chair, Mr. Chairman, ruled that we could not compare this Government to anything eke. I readily concur in that ruling, because, if we are to compare one thing to another, the comparison must be to a thing that 
exists or has existed before. Well, there was never anything, in the heavens above or in the earth beneath or in the waters under the earth, like this Government; therefore we cannot compare it to anything at all. So that I absolutely concur in the ruling of your predecessor in the Chair; I think he was quite right. Nevertheless, although the Government cannot be compared to anything that we know of, the Minister of Finance has a very great responsibility, and to a very great extent he deals with the everyday life of the 9,000,000 people in this country, and he should not discharge that responsibility in the indifferent and jaunty manner, if I may use the expression, which characterizes him when dealing with such matters. Possibly it is a mannerism of the minister, and perhaps, after he gets in the privacy of his chamber and1 closes the door and puts himself in the attitude of prayer, if ever he does that, he may have serious moments; but before us he manages splendidly to throw off every appearance of care in regard to the various onerous duties with which he is charged. He says that these goods are to be marked in a conspicuous place. I rather congratulate him on that because he evidently did not pay very much attention to the criminal legislation which was going through the House this afternoon in relation to the punishment of spanking. I think he should know more about spanking than he does. In regard to that question there was a good deal of dictionary research as to where the spanking was to be applied. I shall not go into the details of that matter, but I would ask the minister to look over the Bill as it was attempted to be put through the House. In that case the spanking was not necessarily to be on a conspicuous place. I h<?pe that before the terms of that Bill apply to the Department of Finance the minister will abandon this proposed legislation and leave us where we were. For the last fifty years, the minister must not forget, we have got along splendidly without this legislation. The minister will remember that we now have customs duties, excise duties, sales tax, business tax, income tax, dumping tax, and now this stamping tax. Now .many of these taxes were brought on by reason of the war, and I do not blame my hon. friend for them. But the war is over now, and we should be pointing the trade of this country, the operations of every industry, as much as possible into the open sea and away from the rocks, difficulties and embarrassments of the war.

We should be getting away from these restrictions until we get out of some of our other difficulties. After we get away from the sales tax, the dumping tax, and all the rest of it, after we get free from the embarrassments of the war taxation and are more at liberty, perhaps the minister might find it necessary to put a few more fences around the trade of this country; but for the present does not the minister think we have troubles enough and new conditions enough that he is imposing on the trade of Canada without adding this restriction? I seriously ask the minister if he does not think-having got along without such impediments for the last fifty years, or even since Confederation -that we could do without this one until we are prepared to drop some of the other embarrassments and taxes which surround the trade of Canada at the present time?

I do not want to delay the minister one moment. If he is determined to go on with this, I should be the last to resort to anything that had even the appearance pf obstruction. But there was one point in his reply to me which filled me with apprehension, and I want to impress it upon him. I want to do it by reminding him that last year I told him that in my humble view certain consequences would result from certain taxes. Well, at the time he did not see it my way, which shows that just for once I saw a little further than he did, because long before his next Budget he gave up the taxes. Now he admits that in regard to these taxes he has already had complaints from importers. I think I understood from my hon. friend that complaints have begun to come in before these marks have gone on, before the law is even in operation. It takes time for these things to make themselves felt and it is for legislators, especially (ministers in the Government of a country, to see fvhat the result of their action is going to be, and not to wait until the trouble ensues:	It
is their duty to prevent trouble-to foresee it if possible. Those importers who are complaining now may just have a little more foresight than the other importers of the country, and if they foresee it, and we fear it, it may be that before this marking has gone very far all the importers will be complaining. After that your goods have to pass from the importers to the retailers, and it may be that the retailers will meet some of these troubles that we fear. All these vexatious interferences with trade must fall somewhere, and they will fall on the people concerned. Now that is my fear. Is it getting any revenue for the country? It will never get a revenue for the country when it is evaded. I cannot see that the good to the consumer is going to compensate for the possible trouble and vexation to importers, retailers and consumers combined. Now I am warning the minister what he may look for in my judgment. It has not got into the retail trade yet, much less has it got to the consumer; but as to the consumer, my honest fear is that it is upon me and men like me that the thing will land. I want to tell the minister that with western prices at the rates so much dwelt upon, with the prices the farmers are getting for their stuff we cannot spend much more. The day will come when, if we want to wear boots and stockings, we will have to cut up some of these cheap sacks the minister is talking about and wrap our feet up in them. But what good will that do the trade of the country? We have to facilitate the communications and dealings of the people with one another. However, I do not want to expatiate upon it. I have explained to the minister my fears, and if he is determined to go on we must take our medicine. It is the aftermath of the war, and the minister is part of that aftermath.

Before the clause passes I would like to inquire from the minister if I understand him right when he said that the goods would be marked with the place of manufacture from which they were shipped by the exporters.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The country of origin, wherever they are made.

That means that if a man is importing goods from the United States the marking is done in that country? Now let us examine and see how far we get with that. You give an order to a retailer * and he orders from a firm in the United States, or in Great Britain, or in some other country, and these goods arrive. Let us read the section my hon. friend has placed before the committee:
That all goods imported into Canada which are capable of being marked, stamped, branded, ur labelled without injuiy, shall be marked, stamped, branded or labelled in legible English or French words, in a conspicuous place that shall not be covered or obscured by any subsequent attachments or arrangements, so as to indicate the country of origin. Said marking, stamping, branding, or labelling shall be as nearly indelible and permanent as the nature of the goods will permit.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
"As nearly indelible." Then he goes on and provides a penalty. I would like to ask my hon. friend to let his mind take him into a court of law and have the lawyers and judges there discussing this question. When a man is brought before the courts for the breaking of the law and expecting a penalty to be imposed, I would like him to imagine the court construing and interpreting the words "said marking, stamping, branding or labelling shall be as nearly indelible and permanent as the nature of the goods will permit." Then again, after these goods come into the country who is going to suffer the penalty? The manufacturer in the country of origin must mark them and if he does not do so he is liable to a penalty. Now, where are you going to get him to impose that penalty? The condition of affairs is one that is of very little importance to the country. As has already been said, it is a most annoying and vexatious arrangement to importers and dealers, but it means nothing to the revenue of the country. Fancy discussing such legislation in the last week or two of the session. Yesterday afternoon, last night, and this afternoon the House was considering a Bill providing how a man should have his dog's tail cut off. That is one of the weighty policies we have been discussing here for the last two days. Now my hon. friend the Minister of Finance after bringing down his Budget proposals very late in the session-much later than they should have been brought down-comes along with a Bill providing for restraint of trade, for that is practically what it means. It means nothing to the country, it means nothing to the Government, it means nothing but trouble and annoyance to everybody concerned, and directly concerned, in the trade of Canada. When I go into a store to buy a pair of boots I do not look inside the footwear to see who made them. If I go in to buy a pair of socks I do not care whether ihey are made in England or the United States-I want the socks and I get them. Ninety-nine out of every hundred men in the country do exactly the same thing. What difference does it make to me who made my boots, or my socks, or my suspenders, or any other article in connection with my wardrobe? It does not matter to anybody. The trouble is that the Minister of Finance, in making jobs for somebody, has surrounded himself with men who are determined to raise trouble for the people of this country. If we had a few more men of common sense and judgment these matters would be dealt with properly and 
sanely. Instead of that men who have been selected are causing trouble and disturbance among the people. It is because of such legislation as this that the country is in a state of unrest and dissatisfaction, and the people are being annoyed and embarrassed by agents of the Government in every possible way. Every day of the session some little picayune thing is brought up by the Government which means nothing to the advantage of the country, but entails great annoyance and vexation to the people who have to deal with the Government and its officials.

I was rather interested in the statement made by the Minister of Finance that these goods should be marked in the country of origin. But unfortunately the Government of Canada has no way of fining the manufacturer if he fails to mark his goods, and the fine falls upon the importer here. We realize that these goods must be marked before they enter Canada, otherwise the customs officer will not pass them at the port of entry. The importer orders his goods and expects them to be marked, but they arrive here not marked. Whose fault is it? It is not the fault of the importer, but he is fined a thousand dollars or sentenced to a year in jail, or possibly both, for the fault of a man whom the Government of this country have no jurisdiction over. That looks to me like a very great hardship on the importer. Firms in the United States and other countries send their travellers to Canada, and they book traders orders for goods. The importer does not see those goods before they enter this country, he has no way of ascertaining whether they are properly marked, but if they are not properly marked, but if no fault of his own, he is fined or imprisoned. This is a very serious thing and should have the earnest consideration of the minister.
Some hon. MEMBERS : Carried.

In justice to the representations that have been made to-night in reference to this matter, I do not think that members behind the Minister of Finance should be in such a hurry, crying "carried". I notice the hon. member for North Simcoe acting like a parrot or a phonograph all night-so frequently does he utter the word "carried". If he continues to read the paper he has before him we will get along much better I think.
The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) is not in his seat just now, but I think he will agree with me,-at least so

far as he is permitted to do so as a Government supporter-that this Bill is bound to cause no end of trouble. He is a manufacturer himself, and possibly is regarded as one of those who have not been objecting to the measure. But getting down to the real issue, I do not see that even our own manufacturers will stand to gain very much by this unnecessary piece of legislation. As a matter of fact, I fancy that 75 per cent of the goods imported at the present time are branded with the country of origin, although that in itself is not always reassuring. The hon. member for Guys-borough said a few moments ago that he had received a penholder from the distribution office branded as being made in the United States. I have in my hand a pencil I received this afternoon from the distribution office marked "British made". But the name of the manufacturer may or may not indicate that he is of British citizenship-E. W-o-l-f-f. That does not indicate an English name to my mind, although the purchaser of this pencil would be buying it with the understanding that it was made by a citizen of Great Britain.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon.
member will allow me, does he think that a good state of affairs?
What is wrong with it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon.
member is saying, Mr. Chairman, that he does not believe that that pencil is British made, that somebody has so branded it for the purpose of selling it as an article of British manufacture. The hon. member suspects that it is a German pencil, and that the branding is being done for the purpose, if he chooses to follow it out, of getting around the British preferential tariff, and therefore is a fraud. We ought to try and stop fraud, but there is no law at present which does enable us to stop it. This law may help us to stop such fraud, and I hope it will.

I think my
hon. friend may be mistaken. The name "Wolff" is a very common Jewish name, and unless he has absolute knowledge that the maker is not a British subject, it is rather unjust to cast a doubt on his bona tides.

The point I make is
that this branding is no absolute guarantee that the pencil is of British manufacture.

The quality
of the stuff is there.
250i

In my judgment the
point is debatable. The fact that an article is branded "British made" does not always indicate that it is so. Therefore as a guarantee it is of no value.
That is the point.

Then there is the matter of expense; I do not know where this is going to stop. Last night we were discussing the depreciation allowed on foreign currency, and the Bill then under consideration provided for a fifty per cent depreciation. That means that merchandise coming from Central Europe will pay six times the existing tariff, and in addition we must take into account freight and insurance, and also something not mentioned by the minister, the rise in British exchange during the last three or four months, running anywhere from ten to eighteen per cent. The result is that you have absolutely prohibited importations from those countries. Therefore a Bill of this kind is useless, because there will be no importations under the provisions that the minister is attempting to put through this House.
Now, taking up the question of marking goods, the Bill we are considering gives no indication of how goods are to be marked or branded, except that it is to be done in a conspicuous place. Dress goods, silks, laces, embroideries, woollen goods, ginghams, serges, linens-these generally are all sold by the yard. Are these goods to be branded on the end or on the selvage? The Bill gives no information and we are left entirely in the dark. We have been simply asked to pass a blank order for the Customs Department to deal with. I insist that it is not safe legislation for the representatives of the people to pass, and we should not be asked to endorse it. I am not attempting to obstruct this measure. I simply want to see it pass through this House as near perfect as possible, for I do not want Parliament to develop into a manufactory of lawsuits among the business interests of this country, but I am sure that if this measure is enacted it will, as I have already said,be the source of no end of trouble. I suppose the legal fraternity in the House would not object to more lawsuits, but it is as patent as the nose on a man's face that that would be the result of placing this Bill on the statute hook. It is too open and ill-considered, and while the lawyer may be glad to see such legislation passed, I appeal to men of common sense in the House and ask them to

say who in their opinion is to mark these imported goods and where. Where are goods made up in detail to be marked? A thousand and one cases will come up in the customs offices each year. Who is to decide all these details? And what is there in it for the consumer? Absolutely nothing. The consumer is well able to judge whether or not certain merchandise is suitable for purchase. If he were not, I do not see how the Government could deal with the matter. Some one has asked, who will pay the cost? Of course, the buyer will pay it, as he always does. This branding cannot be done for nothing. The minister has referred to certain articles which are already branded, but I would point out that these brands are not indelible; they disappear with the first washing. But the branding required under this Act is to be indelible; it will not be removable; it will lessen the selling qualities of the merchandise. This Bill will be an obstacle to trade, it is harmful, it is pernicious; it is absolutely unnecessary. In short, it is pure humbug and will accomplish no good, but will rather raise no end of trouble from one end of the country to the other. Will the minister tell us just what prompted this legislation and what good he hopes to accomplish by it?

When I came into the
chamber at eight o'clock one of the Government supporters was asking the Government to amend the Criminal Code so as to permit the cutting off of dogs' tails. We are considering the last clause of this Bill, and I have been hoping during the last two hours that some supporter of the Government would ask that this clause be cut off; I am quite sure that the Government would find it an even less serious loss than would be the loss of a small dog's tail, because the provision is no value to the country, of no value to the Government. It is simply a nuisance, of no practical value to any one. The minister has not attempted to give any reason why this legislation should be adopted. Every member who has spoken on it has pointed out the trouble and inconvenience that will result from it and the restrictions of trade that will be brought about. The minister seems to realize that the people have no confidence in the Government, and the Government apparently have no confidence in the people, because they are afraid to let ordinary grown-up men-anywhere from twenty to seventy years of age-to walk into a store and buy merchandise without the Government first

looking it over and putting a stamp on it to tell the buyer where it is made-as if that could have any bearing on the value of the commodity. It seems to me so foolish, so nonsensical and so silly that I am surprised that the minister's good sense has not already caused him to ask that the clause be dropped and that the Bill be passed with as little harm in it as possible. Surely the minister must know that we have enough restrictive legislation in this country. We have enough fraternalism, enough of treating every one as the ward of the Government. Let us have a little liberty and freedom in the future; let us have lessyof this restriction. In view of the character of this proposed legislation, Mr. Chairman, and in view of the fact that no hon. member to your right will make the motion, I will move that the clause be struck out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A motion that a clause be struck from a Bill has been ruled out of order on many occasions because it is a negative motion. There is a motion now before the Committee that the clause be adopted, and hon. members who desire to have it stricken from the Bill have the opportunity of voting against that motion.

I would not like this subject to be passed over without a word or two being said in the nature of a reply to the remarks made by the last speaker. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) said Canada has her burdens to bear and her obligations to meet in the form of the heavy debt which is the outcome of the war. As a Canadian I appreciate the value to the farmer of the great home market that Canada furnishes to the products of the farm. It is said that eighty per cent of the farm products of this country are sold in the home market. It is recognized that the home market is the best market for any country. That home market is afforded by the employees in factories and other consumers-by all who are not producers and who get their livelihood in the industrial establishments of the country. At this time, when all the countries of the world are making efforts to command their own trade as best they can, the occasion is opportune for men in this House who believe in Canadian trade to stand up and resent arguments such as those which have been advanced by the hon. member for Pontiac. While we talk in this House about the natural resources of the country it is worth our while to remember that those natural resources would be of no use if

they were not worked out into finished products, the bulk of them for sale to the home consumer and the surplus to he sent abroad. I often think that when we talk of natural resources we are apt to forget the greatest resource of all, the man power and the woman power of the country. That man power and woman power we find most employed on the farms and in the factories. Is it worth while, through the furnishing of that home market, to increase the stability both of our farming and our industrial activities? It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say they would prefer to have the goods of Austria sent into this country and to be sold in competition with the work of our men and our women in our factories and industrial establishments. But I take a totally opposite view. I take the view as a Canadian that it is the duty of this Parliament to look after the humane power of this country, to see that every man and every woman, every girl and every boy of working age is furnished as far as possible with employment.
Are these people furnished with work now?

They are furnished with work now to a greater extent than is the case in any other industrial country. It is true that there is some unemployment in Canada, but I ask the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's to point to any country in the world where there is not more distress, more destitution, more poverty, more hunger, more trouble-labour trouble particularly-than there is in Canada to-day. It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to refer to the conditions now, but I say that now is the time, when there are troubles, for the Government to lay down a sane fiscal and economic policy, a policy which has in view the employment of our workers and which aims to avoid the glutting of our market by the products of foreign countries. We want a policy which will free us from the competition \>f the cheap labour of Austria, Germany and other foreign countries-which, by the way, are very much worse off, through their own fault, of course, than Canada is. But for my part, I say that it is the duty of this Government to take every reasonable precaution, apart from the inconveniences that are talked about. Let us suffer some inconveniences, let us employ a few more men, if that is necessary, to insure that foreign goods shall not be put into this market in competition with the Canadian
product by deceit ana false marking. Let us see what we have to meet. I give the Government and particularly the Minister of Finance credit for standing up for Canadian labour, American workingmen and women throughout the whole country, and for the industrial life of this country.
Americans?
Canadians, I mean.
Oh, oh.
They are the best type of American on this continent, so that I am not far wrong.

The hon. member for
South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) has given to the Minister of Finance some very good reasons for reconsidering what he has done. I will admit that the remarks of the hon. member for South Renfrew have been possibly a little harsh, but after all, they have not been any more so with regard to the action of the Minister otf Finance than were the hon. member's references to the lawyers in the House. I think he stated that, no doubt, lawyers would be glad of any litigation that might result from the operation of this clause in the legislation. Then he said: "But I make my appeal to men of common sense." That was rather an unkind thing to say of the lawyers. While I understand the minister's object-and I think it is a perfectly laudable and worthy one-in his effort to place this regulation upon the statute book, while I believe that in theory it is absolutely correct that Canadian business should be protected, that the Canadian people should have some means of knowing what they are buying, is he not attracting too much importance to that theory and forgetting that its working out in practice will cause more trouble than the advantages to be gained from this law? I believe that is the case. It is not worth while; we have enough troubles of our own as the matter stands now. It is quite true that the business men of Canada have many troubles in these days, and we should do all we can to relieve them of any unnecessary worries, whereas this law will certainly provide many worries. I do not want to rub in the difficulties that the minister experienced in connection with the luxury tax; but I believe that when he looks back upon the operation of that tax, he will admit that if he had known last year what he knew a little later, he would not have applied the luxury tax, and, I

am afraid he will have the same experience in this case. I hope I am not putting him into such a frame of mind as to cause him to be absolutely antagonistic to what I suggest, namely, that he do not lose sight of the fact that while the theory may be right, the practical operation is not in the public interest. I presume he may dislike to amend this legislation in face of the criticism directed against him, and While the criticism has been somewhat harsh, I believe there is a good deal in what has been said by members on this side. While he may dislike to make a change in the face of criticism, to change one's mind in the light of new knowledge is not an evidence of inability nor is it to his discredit, but is rather a tribute to his intelligence and wisdom than a sign of weakness. I wish the minister would seriously consider whether that clause should not be struck out in the interest of merchants and the public generally.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think hon. gentlemen can say that I am at all backward in taking the advice of the House on everything that I can, or that I am at all slow in accepting amendments. I have been blamed in that I have been too ready to accept amendments from hon. gentlemen opposite.
By whom?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By hon. gentlemen opposite. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will remember the debate last year when it was said that I was ready to accept amendments. The idea is that I am ready to accept anything which, in my honest judgment, can improve any legislation that I am framing. That is all by the way. My hon. friend (Mr. Euler) is interested in button-workers in Kitchener. Those button-workers were here not very long ago, asking for a very much increased duty. They did not get it. They thought that they should have an opportunity of meeting fair competition, that people buying their buttons' should know where they came from. I should like to ask the hon. gentleman if he agrees with the button-workers.
Do the button-workers ask that each button be stamped with the place of origin?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course not.

That is exactly what you will find the law will be in its practical working out. I am in accord with the object that the minister seeks to obtain,

but I believe that it is not worth while, because he will find the disadvantages far outweigh the advantages.

I was going to suggest to the minister that sub-clause 2 of this clause be so amended that it will read that the section comes into force upon proclamation by the Govenor in Council. I have listened to all the discussion upon this clause for the last two or three hours, and I am more convinced than ever that this clause is absolutely without merit. It contains the elements of considerable annoyance to the Canadian people. I doubt very much if the minister would proclaim this clause effective if he gives it a little further reflection, and I believe that will be the judgment of the Canadian people if they have an opportunity of studying the section a little further.

I would like to support the proposal of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), for another reason, namely, that the time is short. October 1 is not very far away; it is only about five months from now, and in many lines of trade orders are given fully six months ahead. Orders are taken in the spring for fall delivery, and it might be necessary to have the law before the manufacturers as quickly as possible when goods are not manufactured in this country. The difficulty would be obviated if the suggestion of my hon. friend from Halifax were accepted.

One other point which I wish to call to the minister's attention again is in reference to the penalty clause. I understand that this legislation has been drafted pretty much after the form of the Act in force in the United States. I understand too that the minister, in drafting this penalty clause, omitted one word that is included in the American Act. In my judgment that is a very important word in this connection, and I should like the minister to concede at least the inclusion of this particular word. If the Act in the United States has any virtue, and it has been in operation there since 1913, I think it should be adopted in its entirety here. I would suggest to the minister that he insert the word "fraudulently" in the 14th line, on page 6 of the Bill, between the words "shall" and "violate." As the Act stands now, any person who innocently violated its provisions would be liable to the penalty, and the magistrate would have no discretion

in the matter. I would like this concession from the minister.

I would like to endorse the suggestion of my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) as to the date the Act shall come into force. The goods now being manufactured were ordered last spring, and they will be shipped about September 1 or October 1. I would suggest that the date of coming into force be postponed from October to January.
I beg to move that the word "fraudulently" be inserted in the 14th line between the words "shall" and "violate."

If my hon. friend
would take any advice from me, I would suggest that he use the word "wilfully," which is in nearly all statutes of this kind. There would then be some protection, but as the Bill now stands the magistrate has no discretion at all.

I am quite willing to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend, and I move accordingly.
Amendment negatived.
